docs.text:
The wiki for the UF Autonomy Park and the SCC Lab: our robots, hardware, networks, and software.

Start Here Autonomy Park SITL Autonomy Park GitHub SCC Lab Website

docs.title: Jetsons
docs.text:
Draft. Not a complete inventory. No one has counted the Jetsons yet. Only the Jetsons with reserved IP addresses are listed. Written by Max Gardenswartz, Wyatt Cross, Willie WarkeUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy Park

At a glance

What the Jetsons are, how to use one that is already set up, and how to flash a new Jetson Orin Nano with JetPack 6.0 rev 2. The full count and labels are still to be done.

A Jetson lets a robot run high-compute autonomous programs on board, instead of relying only on its low-power computer for low-level control (for example, a flight controller). Each Jetson is a full computer that runs Ubuntu. The Ubuntu release cannot be upgraded the normal way, because it is bundled in a JetPack version. We currently use JetPack 6.0 rev 2 (see Software We Use).

No Wheels for Python JAX

The Jetsons do not have prebuilt wheels for Python's jax library.

docs.title: How Many Are There
docs.text:
• Jetson Orin Nanos: about 30. Most are set up, but they are not all labeled, and no one has counted them. Most of these are for the Homebrews.
  • Orin NX units: the lab also has some. They have not been inventoried.
  • Which model every other Jetson is: Unknown.

docs.title: Use a Jetson That Is Already Set Up
docs.text:
Most Jetsons are already flashed. To use one, connect it to Ethernet and SSH in, finding its IP address on the Client Devices page of the UniFi gateway. Or connect a keyboard, mouse, and monitor. The Jetsons' IP addresses are on IP Reservations.

A Jetson in the Indoor Lab needs Ethernet with Internet access, or its Wi-Fi changed, to download anything: the Indoor Lab network has no Internet. See Networking Setup (Indoor Lab).

To pull logs and speed up debugging on a Jetson with an AI agent, see AI for Debugging Jetsons.

For a reference video on booting a Jetson from an SSD instead of an SD card, see this video.

docs.title: Flash a New Jetson Orin Nano
docs.text: This flashes a Jetson Orin Nano with JetPack 6.0 rev 2 from a host computer, and installs it on an NVMe SSD.

docs.title: What You Need
docs.text:
• 1 x NVMe SSD (128 GB or more)
  • 1 x Jetson Orin Nano Developer Kit (the target)
  • 1 x Computer (the host) with X86 architecture, Ubuntu 22.04, and 128 GB free space
  • 1 x USB-C data cable
  • 1 x Female-Female jumper wire
  • 1 x Power adapter (included with the Jetson)

docs.title: Install SDK Manager
docs.text: On the host, download and install SDK Manager from NVIDIA. Create a developer account if you do not have one. Then launch it.

docs.title: Insert the NVMe SSD
docs.text:
1. Flip the Jetson, and use the longer slot to insert the SSD.
  2. Insert the SSD at a 45-degree angle.
  3. Press down the free end and tighten the screw to secure it.

docs.title: Connect the Host and the Target
docs.text:
1. Connect the host and target directly using the USB-C data cable.
  2. Use the jumper wire to connect the GPIO pins labeled FC REC and GND (3rd and 4th flat pins from the left).
  3. Connect the target to the power adapter.

Connect in This Order

Connect everything in the order listed above, and keep the jumper wire connected until the final steps.

docs.title: Choose What to Install (SDK Manager Step 1)
docs.text:
On Step 1 of SDK Manager, select:

  • Product Category: Jetson
  • Host Machine: Ubuntu 22.04-x86
  • Target Hardware: Jetson Orin Nano 8GB Dev Kit (Module Number: P3767-0005)
  • SDK Version: JetPack 6.0 (Rev. 2) (includes CUDA 12.2)
  • Additional SDKs: optional

JetPack 6.0 Is Not Selected Automatically

Click on the ... to select to choose JetPack 6.0.

docs.title: Accept the Components (SDK Manager Step 2)
docs.text:
1. On Step 2, check everything on the page. Only Platform Service is optional.
  2. Select Agree and proceed to Step 3.

No Cloud Storage

The target folder should not be linked to cloud storage.

docs.title: Set the Flashing Parameters
docs.text:
In the pop-up window, set:

  • Device: Orin Nano Dev Kit
  • OEM Config: Pre-Config
  • User Name: autonomypark
  • Password: the lab managers on Contacts can give it to you
  • Storage Device: NVMe

docs.title: Flash
docs.text: Click Flash. The system starts downloading. Ignore the connection and disconnection messages.

docs.title: Finish the Installation
docs.text:
When flashing completes, a new page appears. Set:

  • Connector: USB
  • Device: Dev Kit
  • IP Address: it should fill in automatically. If not, use IPv4: 192.165.55.1
  • Credentials: they should be copied automatically
  • Proxy Setting: ignore

Then:

  1. Unplug the jumper wire.
  2. Click Install.
  3. Make sure Dev Kit 0005 is selected, and click OK if prompted.
  4. When the installation completes, return to Step 1 if you need to flash other targets. Otherwise click Finish & Exit.

The Jetson is now ready for commissioning. To log in, connect it to a display and keyboard, or use SSH.

docs.title: Set the IP Before the Hostname
docs.text: Jetsons are finicky. Set the Jetson's IP address before you change its hostname. At the Autonomy Park, see Reserving a Static IP Address.

docs.title: The apt Sources Are Messed Up
docs.text:
If apt update fails because the sources are messed up, run this on the Jetson:

sudo rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
sudo rm -rf /var/cache/app-info
sudo apt clean
sudo apt update

docs.title: Mocap Calibration
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Indoor Lab

At a glance

Recalibrate the Indoor Lab's motion capture when a camera goes down or is replaced. Also covers the Motive version and the USB license key you must never lose.

If a camera goes down or is replaced, the system must be recalibrated.

One Malfunctioning Camera Can Cause Intermittent Problems

A single malfunctioning camera can cause problems that come and go. They can be as rare as one bad frame in 30 minutes, so they are easy to miss. If the mocap data glitches now and then, check every camera before you blame the robot or the software.

docs.title: Motive and Its License Key
docs.text:
The Indoor Lab's motion capture runs on OptiTrack Motive, version 2.0.2.

  • Where it runs: Motive can run on any Windows 11 computer, but it requires the USB license tool (the key) to run. The key is currently in the Windows 11 PC.
  • Old software: Motive 2.0.2 is quite old and may not run on newer versions of Windows. There is a spare key in the lab for an even older version of Motive (version: Unknown), and whether it runs on Windows 11 is Unknown.
  • No reason to change: the current key works, so there is no motivation to change anything until Windows is forced to upgrade (e.g., beyond Windows 11).

Never Remove or Lose the USB License Key

Do not remove the key from the Windows 11 PC. If you lose the key, all access to Motive is lost, and a new key is needed. A new key costs $999: see Motive pricing.

Software License Info

docs.title: Mocap Tutorial Video
docs.text: This video covers the mocap tutorial and the bebop_common autonomy stack for the Bebops.

docs.title: The Cameras
docs.text: The Indoor Lab has 20 OptiTrack Prime 17W cameras mounted. There may be spares, but nobody knows where they are right now.

docs.title: Calibration File for MAE-A 313
docs.text:
The current calibration file is main.cal. It is already on the Motive computer (MAE-MH-BPLKHL2), in C:\Motive 2.02 NCR Calibration Files. This download is a backup copy. It was made in October 2025, and Motive rated its accuracy "Exceptional". Its mean error is Unknown.

A calibration belongs to one space and one camera arrangement. A new space needs a new calibration.

Download the Calibration File

docs.title: Motive Installer
docs.text:
The Motive 2.0.2 installer needs no login to download. Running Motive still needs the USB license key.

Download the Motive 2.0.2 Installer

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Remove all robots with markers from the camera field of view
    • Place the robots in a locker or cover them to avoid interference.
  1. Set the OptiTrack reference
    • Obtain the wand and the OptiTrack calibration square.
    • Place the OptiTrack at the lab coordinate origin.
    • Align the square so its axes match the lab coordinate axes.

  1. Start wanding

    • Launch Motive.
    • Click Start Wanding.
    • Move the wand throughout the lab so that all cameras collect samples. You will see the ring around each camera turn green as it gathers sufficiently many samples

  2. Calculate calibration

    • Continue wanding until each camera collects several thousand samples.
    • Click Calculate.

  3. Apply calibration

    • Click Apply Result.
    • Save the calibration file.

  4. Set ground plane

    • Click Set Ground Plane to finalize the coordinate frame.

docs.title: Radio and RC Setup Guide
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-09Autonomy Park

At a glance

The lab's legacy radio setup (FrSky Taranis X9D+ and X8R), how to someday replace it, and how to flash, bind, and set it up with a FrSky X8R receiver, of which we have two.

This document serves as the official guide to the radio control systems used for the lab's Homebrew drone fleet. Its purpose is twofold: first, to document our current legacy hardware setup for operation and troubleshooting; second, to provide a clear and definitive upgrade path for all future builds.

The RC hobby has undergone significant, and often confusing, technological shifts. Adhering to the procedures and recommendations in this guide will prevent the compatibility issues and time-consuming troubleshooting that have historically plagued this field.

docs.title: Current Lab Standard Configuration
docs.text:
This table details the components of our primary drone control system as of the date above.

Component Manufacturer & Model / Software Name Version & Comments Transmitter (Hardware) FrSky Taranis X9D Plus (non-2019 model) This is our legacy radio. Note that batteries and chargers are no longer produced, marking it as end-of-life. Transmitter (OS) OpenTX v2.3.15. This is the final version of OpenTX; the project is no longer in development. Internal TX Module FrSky XJT ACCST D16 v2.1.0 (FCC). This firmware is on the internal radio module, separate from OpenTX. Receiver FrSky X8R ACCST D16 v2.1.0 (FCC). Must match the transmitter module's protocol, version, and region (FCC). Flight Controller (FC) CubePilot Blue Communicates with the receiver via the S.BUS protocol. FC Firmware PX4 Autopilot v1.16 (or latest stable release). Our standard autopilot software stack. Ground Control Station QGroundControl Used for flight planning, parameter configuration, and real-time monitoring, or configuring the FC via a microUSB cable.

The CubePilot Blue Says ArduPilot

The CubePilot Blue hardware is often associated with ArduPilot, as it is written on the side of it. We use PX4 only, so do not let this decal mislead you. ArduPilot is not part of the CubePilot Blue's model name.

docs.title: Glossary of Essential RC Terminology
docs.text:
Transmitter (TX): The handheld radio controller used by the pilot. It converts stick and switch movements into a digital radio signal. Also called a "radio."

Receiver (RX): A small component on the drone that receives the signal from the transmitter and sends the commands to the Flight Controller.

Binding: The process of creating a unique, exclusive digital link between one transmitter and one receiver. A bound receiver will only respond to its paired transmitter.

Flight Controller (FC): The "brain" of the drone. It takes input from the receiver and sensors (gyros, accelerometers, GPS) to stabilize the aircraft and execute commands.

Firmware: Low-level software that runs on hardware. In our context, this refers to the software on the radio modules (like the XJT's ACCST firmware) and the receiver, which is separate from the transmitter's main operating system (OpenTX).

FrSky: A manufacturer of RC hardware that was once the de facto standard but now represents a legacy ecosystem due to their transition to a modern product line that is expensive and runs entirely proprietary software.

Taranis: A popular series of transmitters made by FrSky, including our lab's X9D Plus model.

XJT: The name of the internal transmitter module inside the Taranis X9D Plus.

OpenTX: The powerful, open-source operating system that runs on Taranis transmitters. Its development is now defunct, with the last version being 2.3.15.

Protocol: The "language" used for wireless communication between the transmitter module and the receiver. Examples include ACCST, ACCESS, and ELRS.

Serial Communication Protocol: The language used for the wired communication between the receiver and the flight controller.

PPM (Pulse Position Modulation): An older, aggregate signal format that encodes multiple PWM channels into a single, analog-style pulse train. While it allows for a single-wire connection between the receiver and flight controller, it suffers from high latency and low resolution compared to modern digital protocols. It is now considered obsolete for performance-oriented drones.

S.BUS (Serial Bus): A digital communication protocol originally developed by Futaba and widely adopted by FrSky. It transmits up to 16 channels of control data from the receiver to the flight controller over a single wire. It is a reliable, one-way protocol for control input only; a separate protocol like S.Port is required for telemetry. It is not deprecated yet, as of October 2025, but is being superseded in modern systems.

FPort (FrSky Port Protocol): A newer, more efficient protocol from FrSky designed to be the successor to the S.BUS and S.Port combination. FPort is a bidirectional protocol that cleverly combines RC control data and telemetry into a single data stream on one wire, simplifying wiring significantly.

IBUS (FlySky Bus): The serial communication protocol used by the manufacturer FlySky. Functionally, it is FlySky's direct equivalent to S.BUS, providing digital channel data from the receiver to the flight controller over a single wire. A separate connection is typically required for telemetry data.

CRSF (Crossfire Protocol): A high-speed, bidirectional protocol developed by Team BlackSheep (TBS) and now used as the standard for ExpressLRS (ELRS). It is renowned for its extremely low latency and high update rates. It natively carries both RC control data and extensive telemetry data in a single packet, making it the current performance standard.

SRXL2 (Spektrum Remote Receiver Link v2): The modern, bidirectional serial protocol from Spektrum. It sends control data, telemetry, VTX control, and ESC data over a single wire. It is a significant improvement over Spektrum's older satellite receiver protocols (DSMX), offering faster speeds and more robust data transmission.

S.Port (Smart Port): A bidirectional digital communication protocol developed by FrSky. Its primary purpose is to connect telemetry sensors (like GPS, voltage, or current sensors) in a daisy-chain configuration, allowing data from all connected sensors to be sent back to the receiver over a single wire. It is also the physical port used to flash firmware onto FrSky receivers, as described in this guide. It should not be confused with S.BUS, which is used to send control channel data from the receiver to the flight controller.

CRSF (Crossfire): A modern, high-speed, bidirectional protocol developed by TBS. It is used by ELRS and other modern systems to send channel data to the FC and receive telemetry data back. This is the successor to S.BUS for all new builds.

Telemetry: Data sent back from the drone's receiver to the transmitter, such as battery voltage or signal strength (RSSI). This data can be displayed on the transmitter's screen or used to trigger audible alerts.

Mode 2: The standard stick configuration in the US. The left stick controls throttle (up/down) and yaw (left/right). The right stick controls pitch (up/down) and roll (left/right).

docs.title: The Legacy System & The Path to Obsolescence
docs.text: Our current FrSky-based system was once the gold standard. However, a series of business and technical decisions by FrSky has rendered the entire ecosystem obsolete. It is critical to understand this history to appreciate why we must transition away from it.

docs.title: The Fracture of the FrSky Ecosystem
docs.text:
Around 2019, FrSky made changes that created widespread chaos:

  • ACCST v1 vs. v2: FrSky released an ACCST v2 firmware update. This update was not backward-compatible with v1. This means a v2 transmitter cannot bind to a v1 receiver, and vice versa. This created a huge burden on users to ensure every component was on the correct, matching version.
  • The ACCESS Protocol: FrSky then introduced a new, completely locked-down protocol called ACCESS. This move was intended to block competitors and force users into a new, proprietary ecosystem, alienating much of the community.
  • Regional Firmware (FCC vs. LBT): To comply with regulations, all protocols also come in two regional flavors: FCC (for the US and most of the world) and LBT (for the EU). These are also incompatible with each other.

This leaves users with a confusing matrix of protocol, version, and region that must all match perfectly to achieve a successful bind.

docs.title: Why We Must Upgrade
docs.text:
Our Taranis X9D Plus and X8R system is now a dead end for several practical reasons:

  • End-of-Life Software: OpenTX development is frozen. It will receive no new features or bug fixes.
  • Hardware Scarcity: FrSky no longer produces batteries or chargers for the Taranis X9D Plus. Once our current hardware fails, it will be difficult and expensive to replace.
  • Poor Documentation: FrSky's official website (https://www.frsky-rc.com/) is the only source for firmware but is impossible to find with a search engine and the documentation is terse, sometimes illegible, and imprecise. (Do not use retail sites like (https://www.frskyna.com/) for official files).
  • Cost: New FrSky transmitters are significantly more expensive than modern, superior alternatives.

For all these reasons, while we will maintain our current setup, any hardware failure or new drone project will mandate a switch to the modern standard.

docs.title: The Modern Standard & Recommended Upgrade Path
docs.text:
The RC community has moved to a fully open-source, higher-performance ecosystem. This is the required standard for all new lab purchases.

GUI Software: EdgeTX: The community-led successor to OpenTX. It is actively developed and supports modern hardware. Protocol: ExpressLRS (ELRS): This is the new open standard for RC links.

docs.title: Recommended Hardware
docs.text:
• Transmitter: RadioMaster TX16S or RadioMaster Boxer, with an internal ELRS module. These offer superior features to the Taranis for a fraction of the cost of new FrSky gear. A budget of under $300 is sufficient.
  • Receiver:
    • For PWM Output: The RadioMaster ER8 2.4GHz ELRS PWM Receiver is a direct, modern replacement for the FrSky X8R, offering 8 physical servo ports.
    • For Serial Connection: For builds that only require a digital connection to the FC (most of our builds), a smaller receiver like the RadioMaster RP4TD ExpressLRS is excellent but requires soldering.
    • Always choose the FCC version when purchasing.

These components use the CRSF serial protocol to communicate with the flight controller, which is supported by our CubePilot Blue and PX4.

docs.title: Procedures for the Current System (FrSky Taranis X9D+)
docs.text:
This section covers the essential procedures for operating our legacy FrSky equipment.

Remove the Propellers

Always remove the propellers from the drone before performing any setup, binding, or firmware update.

docs.title: Flashing Firmware on the X8R Receiver
docs.text:
Firmware for the internal XJT module and the X8R receiver must match (ACCST D16 v2.1.0 FCC). You can flash the receiver directly from the Taranis.

Required: - 3 appropriately colored Dupont cables. A servo cable will not work because the cable orientations do not match. - The correct receiver firmware .frk file downloaded from https://www.frsky-rc.com/ and placed on the transmitter's SD card in the [FIRMWARE] folder.

Verify Your Firmware File

The firmware file for the X8R receiver is different from the one for the transmitter's internal XJT module. They are not interchangeable. Flashing the wrong firmware to the receiver can prevent it from binding or render it inoperable. Always double-check that you are selecting the X8R firmware file (and not the XJT file) before you select "Flash external module."

Procedure: 1. Power everything off. Ensure the receiver is disconnected from the flight controller. 2. Connect the servo cable to the receiver's S.Port (not S.BUS or any PWM channel). 3. Connect the other end of the servo cable to the pins in the external module bay on the back of the Taranis. Ensure the signal, power, and ground pins are correctly oriented. Look this up for the Taranis! The X8R's pins are labeled. 4. Turn on the Taranis transmitter. 5. Long-press the MENU button to access Radio Setup. Press PAGE to navigate to the SD-HC CARD screen. 6. Navigate to the [FIRMWARE] folder and select the correct X8R firmware file. 7. Long-press the ENT button. A context menu will appear. 8. Select "Flash external module." The flashing process will begin. Do not disconnect power. 9. Once the "Flashing successful" message appears, you can power everything down and disconnect the cable.

docs.title: Flashing Firmware on the Internal XJT Module
docs.text:
Just as the receiver requires specific firmware, the transmitter's internal XJT module must also be running the correct version to ensure a successful bind. The process is nearly identical to flashing a receiver, but you select a different option in the radio's menu.

Verify Your Firmware File

The firmware file for the internal XJT module is different from the one for the X8R receiver. They are not interchangeable. Flashing receiver firmware to the transmitter module (or vice-versa) is possible and there are no safeguards to stop you. Always double-check that you are selecting the XJT firmware file for this procedure.

Required: - The correct XJT module firmware .frk file downloaded from frsky-rc.com and placed on the transmitter's SD card in the [FIRMWARE] folder.

Procedure: 1. Turn on the Taranis transmitter. 2. Long-press the MENU button to access Radio Setup. Press PAGE repeatedly to navigate to the SD-HC CARD screen. 3. Navigate into the [FIRMWARE] folder and locate the correct XJT firmware file you downloaded. 4. Highlight the file and long-press the ENT button to open the context menu. 5. Select the option "Flash internal module." 6. The flashing process will begin. Do not power off the transmitter. 7. Once the "Flashing successful" message appears, press EXIT. It is good practice to power cycle the transmitter.

docs.title: Binding the X8R to the Taranis
docs.text:
1. Power everything off.
  2. Physically disconnect the receiver from the flight controller.
  3. Turn on the Taranis transmitter. Use the PAGE button to navigate to the MODEL SETUP screen for your drone.
  4. Scroll down to the "Internal RF" section.
  5. Set Mode to D16.
  6. Set Receiver No. to a unique number for this model (e.g., 01).
  7. Select the [Bind] option and press ENT. Select “CH 1-8 Telemetry [ON]” or a similar option. Telemetry is not mandatory, though. The transmitter will start chirping, indicating it is in bind mode.
  8. Connect the LiPo battery to the drone. Wait a few seconds for it to boot up.
  9. On the X8R receiver, press and hold the F/S (Failsafe) button. You will need a pen or screwdriver to reach it.
  10. While still holding the F/S button, connect the 3-pin cable to the S.BUS slots (not the massive array of PWM slots) on the receiver. Connect the other end RC slot on the CubePilot Blue flight controller. The receiver's two LEDs will light up: solid red and solid green. After a moment or two, the green LED should start flashing, indicating a successful bind. The red will still be solid. You can now release the F/S button.
  11. On the transmitter, press EXIT to stop the binding process.
  12. Power cycle the drone by disconnecting and reconnecting the LiPo battery (or by disconnecting and reconnecting the cable between it and the flight controller).
  13. The receiver should now show a solid green LED, indicating a successful and active link.
  14. You may now power off the transmitter and drone in any order. If Telemetry was enabled, the transmitter will warn you a receiver is still connected before powering off if you are powering it off first.

docs.title: Initial Setup in OpenTX & PX4
docs.text:
• Model Profiles: In OpenTX, each aircraft has its own "model" profile. This profile stores all settings, including switch assignments, trims, and which receiver number it's bound to. Switching models in OpenTX makes the transmitter look for a different receiver; it does not unbind the previous one. Note: Model profiles cannot be directly transferred between different transmitter models (e.g., Taranis to RadioMaster) or even between different Taranis models running the same OpenTX version due to hardware differences.
  • Switches: To use a switch, it must be configured in three places in OpenTX: HARDWARE, MIXER, and OUTPUTS.
  • Sounds: Audio files for alerts are stored on the SD card in the [SOUNDS] folder. These can be assigned to switch positions or events in the SPECIAL FUNCTIONS menu. You may consider adding your own if the built-in one are imprecise for your needs. The author’s favorite is the Open-TX-Portal-Voice-Pack.
  • PX4 Flight Modes: In QGroundControl, under Vehicle Setup > Flight Modes, you will assign switches to flight modes. The required modes for our operations are:
    • Stabilized: Manual roll/pitch/yaw rate control, with auto-leveling. Throttle is manual.
    • Attitude: Manual roll/pitch/yaw angle control. More intuitive than Stabilized. Throttle is manual.
    • Position: The drone holds its position (latitude, longitude, altitude) using GPS when sticks are centered.
    • Hold: The drone will stop and hold its current position.
    • Land: The drone will automatically land at its current position.
  • Safety Features:
    • Arm/Disarm: Assign a switch in PX4 to arm and disarm the motors. This is a critical safety function.
    • Failsafe: The receiver failsafe must be set to ensure the drone does not fly away if the signal is lost. For PX4, the failsafe should be set to "No Pulses" on the receiver. PDF for setting X8R failsafe

Do Not Use Return Mode

Do not use the default "Return to Land" or "Return to Launch" mode on the drone. Our operational areas often have obstacles that make this unsafe. The designated failsafe action is either Land or Hold.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
docs.text:
Q: My receiver has a solid green light, but QGroundControl shows no stick/switch inputs? A: This is almost always a wiring issue. The X8R must be connected to the flight controller via the single S.BUS port, not the main block of PWM channel pins. Ensure the 3-wire cable runs from the X8R's S.BUS port to the correct RC Input port on the CubePilot.

Q: I switched models on my Taranis and the drone disconnected. Is it unbound? A: No. The receiver remains bound to the transmitter's internal module. OpenTX model profiles are associated with a "Receiver No." When you switch models, the transmitter starts trying to talk to a different receiver number. Simply switch back to the correct model profile to reconnect.

Q: Do I need a 16-channel receiver to get 16 channels to the flight controller? A: No. The number in a receiver's name (e.g., ER8) typically refers to the number of physical PWM (servo) outputs. A digital serial protocol like S.BUS or CRSF sends all 16 channels over a single wire to the flight controller, regardless of how many PWM ports the receiver has.

Q: What do I do if I sever a receiver antenna? A: Never solder a severed antenna. This will alter its length and impedance, leading to unpredictable signal loss and potential flyaways that are impossible to debug. Replace the antenna with an identical part. If a replacement is not available, replace the entire receiver. It is not worth the risk.

  • Amazon.com: Good for generic supplies but verify sellers for specialized hardware.

docs.title: Disclaimer & Final Recommendations
docs.text:
This guide is a living document intended to serve as a starting point for operating and upgrading the lab's RC equipment. While every effort has been made to ensure accuracy, the RC hobby is complex, and legacy hardware, in particular, is prone to unique and unforeseen failures.

Treat this document as a reference, not an infallible set of instructions. During the creation of this guide, for example, the Taranis X9D+'s internal SD card failed without warning and a new one had to be procured. Expect the unexpected, and always be prepared to troubleshoot.

If you encounter an issue not covered here, or if a procedure does not yield the expected result, it is crucial to cross-reference information with other resources. Consulting modern YouTube tutorials, searching Google Images for correct wiring diagrams, or asking an AI assistant for clarification can often provide the solution that this document may lack.

docs.title: Learning Resources
docs.text: For general drone building and hardware reviews, the author recommends Joshua Bardwell on YouTube as a highly respected and knowledgeable source.

docs.title: A Note on Procurement
docs.text: To the best of our knowledge, nearly all hobbyist RC hardware is manufactured in China. Be aware that university and grant funding may have restrictions on purchasing electronics from these sources. Plan accordingly.

docs.title: RTK Setup
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy Park

At a glance

RTK corrections come from our Emlid Reach RS3 ground station. Ground robots with an Emlid unit get them over LoRa radio; all other robots get them from the RTKLib caster, never the RS3's embedded caster.

RTK corrections make GPS position centimeter-level accurate, allowing much better precisse handling and repeatability of experiments. We require RTK to guarantee that altitude estimation is accurate enough to prevent collisions with the net. A ground station at a known position sends corrections to the robot, which uses them to remove the GPS error it shares with the ground station.

docs.title: Ground Station
docs.text:
Our ground station is an Emlid Reach RS3. It is configured from the Emlid Flow mobile app.

The Emlid Reach RS3 (product image).

The ground station is mounted at the Autonomy Park main shed (not the storage shed), on the mounting tower seen in the video below.

docs.title: Setting Up
docs.text:
Follow the instructions in the video.

The Emlid is battery powered, and the battery lasts about 24 hours. To charge while using it, plug a USB-C charger into the surge protector in the equipment cabinet next to the mounting tower.

Do Not Break the Equipment Cabinet's Lock

The cabinet requires a key, but the key has been lost. Take the smallest pliers from the toolbox in the main shed and carefully open the cabinet by twisting each of the key slots. Spread the pliers' jaws apart (do not twist the center part).

If you break this piece, all the equipment in the cabinet (for example, the barometer) is no longer weatherproof and will be damaged.

docs.title: Before You Leave
docs.text:
1. Power off the Emlid before unmounting it.
  2. Unmount it.
  3. Put it away in the Emlid RS3's case, with the mounting screw and the LoRa antenna. Do not lose either one.
  4. Close the equipment cabinet.
  5. Take the Emlid inside the main shed before you leave.

Never take the Emlid off the premises of the Autonomy Park.

docs.title: Emlid Flow Settings for Ground Station
docs.text:
Get the Emlid Flow app for your phone.

Emlid Flow on the App Store Emlid Flow on Google Play

Single Is Expected for the Ground Station

The fix status in the upper right of the Emlid Flow app shows Single for the ground station. That is expected, because the ground station has no corrections to receive. It is not expected for the rovers: a rover should not stay on Single once it is receiving corrections.

The receiver is named TOWERBASESTATION in the Emlid Flow app, and joins the UFLAutonomyPark Wi-Fi network. You will not be able to 5 GHz network; that's okay. These are its base settings.

Setting Value Base output 1 TCP server, localhost:9000 Base output 2 LoRa radio, 920.0 MHz, 18.23 kb/s Correction format RTCM3 RTCM3 message 1006 (base position) 0.1 Hz RTCM3 messages 1074, 1084, 1094, 1230 (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, GLONASS biases) 1 Hz RTCM3 message 1124 (BeiDou) Off Coordinates entry method Manual Base marker 29.62840700° N, -82.36057600° E, ellipsoidal height 0.849 m Antenna height 2.174 m

The screenshots below are the same settings in the app.

  • Our Emlid units: four rover units labelled Emlid RS 001 to 004, and one RS3, which is the ground station. All four rovers are RS+ units, and they are configured identically.

docs.title: Emlid Flow Settings for Rovers/Clients
docs.text:
These are the settings of one of the rover Emlid RS+ units in the Emlid Flow app. All four (RS+) are configured identically. While any could be used as a base station, we use them on robots as recipients of RTK corrections ("rovers").

Setting Value Correction input LoRa radio, 920.0 MHz, 18.23 kb/s (shows "Receiving corrections") Wi-Fi UFLAutonomyPark Base output 1 and 2 Off Position streaming 1 Serial, USB to PC, 57600, NMEA Position streaming 2 TCP server, localhost:9001, NMEA

docs.title: How Corrections Reach the Robots
docs.text:
How RTK corrections reach ground robots (LoRa) and quadcopters (local NTRIP and a caster).

There are two ways, depending on the robot:

  • Ground robots with an Emlid unit (for example, an RS) use LoRa radio.
  • All other robots use the RTKLib caster. This includes the quadcopters.

This dual system was not chosen because Wi-Fi or the caster would get saturated with many agents (that is not known). It was chosen to minimize changes to existing configurations.

docs.title: The RTKLib Caster
docs.text:
Corrections are served by RTKLib running on the discovery server computer. An NTRIP client on each quadcopter's companion computer publishes them to <mavros_namespace>/mavros/gps_rtk/send_rtcm. Serving RTK through QGC does not work: see PX4 Configuration.

Use the RTKLib caster, never the RS3's embedded caster.

The caster is already running. For how it was built, see NTRIP Caster for RTK on Quadcopters (reference only).

  • RTKLib version: 2.4.3. It is very stable and has not needed an update since 2020.
  • RTKLib configuration: the access details for getting corrections from the RTKLib caster are in the homebrew_docker repository. They are not published on the wiki. See GitHub Access.
  • Indoor Lab: the Indoor Lab has no RTKLib caster. Nothing indoors needs RTK: the Bebops are the only indoor quadcopters.

docs.title: Knowing the Fix Is Good
docs.text:
What a Good Fix Is for a Quadcopter

A good fix is fix_type 6, always. Read the fix_type entry of <namespace>/mavros/gpsstatus/gps1/raw. When everything works, every single message coming out of MAVROS shows 6 (RTK fixed) while flying around, never less.

This reliability is only tested up to three quadcopters under the current setup: RTKLib on the discovery server computer. Three agents have also been tested with the Emlid RS3's embedded caster, which sends corrections over an individual link to every quadcopter (every local NTRIP client). That is not reliable at all: the fix drops out randomly and intermittently. Even with one agent, flying can reduce the fix to 5 from what it was on the ground, with no recovery and no explanation. Use the RTKLib caster, never the embedded caster.

Wait for the Fix to Reach 6

Getting a fix takes 5 to 15 minutes. Until fix_type reaches 6, expect lots of "Global position estimate invalid" errors. A fix of 5 (RTK float) can make flights unstable, so it is very important to wait for 6 (fixed) before you fly.

The fix should drop to 5 or lower, even for a single frame, only if you hit the ground hard, crash, or the satellites cut out. (The satellites cut out once in 100 flight hours.) Moving fast or changing altitude should never demote the fix.

Multi-agent testing has not been done, so it is unknown whether network traffic, or changing access points, affects the fix.

An Easier Way to Check the Fix

Click the GPS icon in the Fly tab of AMC (Astros) or QGC (Homebrews) to check the RTK fix.

docs.title: Security Cameras
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-03Autonomy Park

At a glance

The Autonomy Park cameras record to a Lorex NVR that keeps only the last 24 hours. Getting good footage out of it is very difficult.

Do Not Count on the Footage

The cameras record to a Lorex NVR. It is very difficult to get good footage from them.

  • Where: the NVR is at 192.168.1.33. You can also reach it with the Home Assistant bookmark in the Chrome browser on the Autonomy Park computer.
  • How long: only the last 24 hours are stored.
  • Replay: replaying footage on the NVR works, but it can skip around unexpectedly.
  • Quality: the video quality is poor.
  • Getting files out: pulling files directly onto a USB stick is nearly impossible.

The other Autonomy Park addresses are on IP Reservations.

docs.title: Wireless Controllers
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-21Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

Use the PlayStation 5 DualSense controllers to drive robots from ROS 2. They connect over Bluetooth on Linux with no setup, which Xbox controllers do not.

Do Not Remove the DualSense Controllers from Their Lab

There is one DualSense controller in the Indoor Lab and one at the Autonomy Park. Neither should be removed from its lab.

docs.title: Our Controllers
docs.text:
Controller Color Where How many Notes Last Updated PlayStation 5 DualSense Wireless Black Indoor Lab 1 Bought in September 2026. Use this one. 2026-10-21 PlayStation 5 DualSense Wireless White Autonomy Park 1 Bought in September 2026. Use this one. 2026-10-21 Xbox 360 Wireless Black Indoor Lab 2 Both work, but both have stick drift. 2026-10-21

The Xbox Wireless Controller on this page always means the third revision, which is different from the Xbox 360 Wireless controllers. The Autonomy Park used to have a third-revision Xbox Wireless Controller. We broke its USB-C port and it became useless (see below), so it was thrown away. The lab has no Xbox Wireless Controllers now.

The PlayStation 5 DualSense Wireless Controller (stock image).

The Xbox Wireless Controller, third revision (stock image). The lab no longer has one.

docs.title: Why the DualSense Is Better for Robotics
docs.text: Both the Xbox Wireless Controller and the PlayStation 5 DualSense Wireless Controller are supported by ROS 2 (for example, by the joy node). The difference is in how they connect to Linux.

docs.title: Bluetooth Works Out of the Box on the DualSense
docs.text:
The Linux kernel has Bluetooth support for the DualSense, so it works over Bluetooth out of the box. It does not even need the latest firmware.

The Xbox Wireless Controller does not have Bluetooth support on Linux out of the box. It apparently must be upgraded to the latest firmware, and that can only be done on Windows. We tried the upgrade on one controller, on multiple computers, and it failed. We did not hard reset the controller to try again. So we never verified whether newer firmware would allow Bluetooth to work on Linux.

When we connected the Xbox Wireless Controller to Linux, it connected and disconnected rapidly, and we could not solve it.

docs.title: Why Bluetooth Matters
docs.text:
• A fallback when USB-C breaks. We broke the USB-C port of a third-revision Xbox Wireless Controller at the Autonomy Park. Without Bluetooth as a fallback, the controller became useless.
  • Fewer cable snags. A cable can snag, and it stresses the USB-C port.

docs.title: Firmware Updates Are Windows-Only
docs.text: Updating the firmware of either controller is only possible with a Windows-only app. Running it with Wine or on Linux is not possible at all. We also tried upgrading a DualSense's firmware on Windows, and that failed too. The DualSense does not need the update.

docs.title: How to Pair a DualSense on Ubuntu
docs.text:
1. Put the DualSense in pairing mode: hold the PS button and the Create button (the small button left of the touchpad) until the light bar flashes.

  2. In a terminal on your computer, open the Bluetooth tool:

    bluetoothctl

  3. At its prompt, start scanning, and find the controller's address in the list:

    scan on

  4. Pair, trust, and connect, using that address:

    pair <controller-mac-address>
trust <controller-mac-address>
connect <controller-mac-address>

Once trusted, the controller reconnects on its own when you turn it on.

docs.title: Run the joy Node
docs.text:
The joy node publishes the controller's buttons and sticks to the /joy topic. Connect the controller over Bluetooth or USB first.

Install the package on your computer, then run the node in a new terminal:

sudo apt install ros-humble-joy

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run joy joy_node

docs.title: Find Which Button Is Which Input
docs.text:
Your robot code reads the buttons and axes arrays of the /joy messages by index. To find the index of each button:

  1. Run the joy node with the controller connected over Bluetooth or USB.

  2. In another terminal, echo the topic:

    source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 topic echo /joy

  3. Press one button at a time. In the buttons list, the value changes from 0 to 1 for that button.

  4. Count the lines of the buttons list down to the changed value. That index is the button's input number.

    The First Line Is Index 0

    Count the first line of the list as index 0, not 1. Counting from 1 makes every button off by one.

The same method works for the axes list: move one stick and count the lines to the value that changes.

docs.title: Chrony Time Sync
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-06Autonomy Park

At a glance

Every computer that runs our ROS 2 nodes syncs its clock with chrony to the discovery server, which serves time to the Autonomy Park network. How to set up the server and the clients.

Every computer that runs ROS 2 nodes for the lab runs chrony: the Homebrew Jetsons, the ground station computers, and the discovery server. The discovery server (192.168.1.201 on the Autonomy Park network) is the time server. It syncs to the internet and serves time to the network. Everything else syncs to it.

This page is adapted from TIME_SYNC.md in homebrew_docker.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• Message ages are computed across machines. MAVROS stamps PX4 data with the Jetson's clock. A node on a ground computer compares that stamp with its own clock, so any offset between the two clocks goes straight into the computed age.
  • Comparing times to the millisecond. To measure the timestamps an offboard program receives, anywhere but on the companion computer, you need chrony. Without it, the times on different computers differ by milliseconds over ROS. That can hide problems such as stale odometry, and it makes experiments harder to replicate.
  • One shared reference. When every machine syncs to the same server, their clocks agree with each other even if the internet is slow or down.
  • No clock jumps after boot. chrony steps the clock only in its first updates after starting (makestep 1 3 in Ubuntu's default config), and slews it gradually afterwards. A jump while MAVROS runs makes it reset its time sync. After a battery pull, a Jetson boots with its clock at 1970 (homebrew05, 2026-10-14: chrony stepped it forward 56.8 years, 22.6 s after boot), so the homebrew_docker container's entrypoint waits until the clock agrees with the time server before starting ROS.
  • Ubuntu's server documentation recommends chrony for serving NTP. systemd-timesyncd, the default client, implements SNTP only and cannot serve time.

Containers need nothing. A container cannot have its own wall clock, so the homebrew_docker container uses the Jetson's clock.

chrony and systemd-timesyncd Conflict

On Ubuntu, installing one removes the other. All the configuration below is new files in /etc/chrony/conf.d/. Ubuntu's chrony.conf includes that directory, and the packaged chrony.conf is never edited.

docs.title: The Discovery Server
docs.text:
Run these on the discovery server computer.

  1. Check the Ubuntu version and whether the firewall is active:

    head -2 /etc/os-release
sudo ufw status

  2. Install chrony:

    sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y chrony

  3. Check that Ubuntu's chrony.conf includes the conf.d directory:

    grep -n confdir /etc/chrony/chrony.conf

    It must print confdir /etc/chrony/conf.d. If it prints nothing, stop: the files below would be ignored.

  4. Serve time to the network, and keep serving it if the internet is lost:

    printf 'allow 192.168.1.0/24\nlocal stratum 10\n' | sudo tee /etc/chrony/conf.d/lan-server.conf

  5. Restart chrony:

    sudo systemctl restart chrony
    • allow 192.168.1.0/24 serves time to the network.
    • local stratum 10 keeps the server answering when the internet is lost. Internet sources are stratum 1 to 3, and chrony's documentation says the local stratum should be larger than the largest stratum expected in the network.

  6. Only if ufw status said active, allow the network to reach the time port:

    sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 123 proto udp

  7. About a minute after the restart, check that it works:

    chronyc sources
chronyc tracking
sudo ss -ulpn | grep ':123 '
    • chronyc sources: one line starts with ^*, the selected internet source.
    • chronyc tracking: Stratum 2 (or 3), a Reference ID naming an internet server, and Leap status : Normal. Reference ID 7F7F0101 with Stratum 10 means the server is on its own clock. That is normal for a few seconds after a restart, and it is what the server does when the internet is down.
    • ss: chronyd is listening on UDP port 123.

docs.title: The Homebrew Jetsons
docs.text: This is part of the first-time setup in the homebrew_docker README (step 1.8). The commands are the same as for a ground computer, below.

docs.title: Ground Computers
docs.text:
Do this on any other computer that runs ROS 2 nodes.

  1. Install chrony:

    sudo apt-get install -y chrony

  2. Point it at the discovery server:

    printf 'server 192.168.1.201 iburst prefer\n' | sudo tee /etc/chrony/conf.d/lab-time-server.conf

  3. Restart chrony and check the sources after 30 seconds:

    sudo systemctl restart chrony
sleep 30
chronyc sources
    • iburst sends a burst of requests at startup, so the first sync takes seconds, not minutes.
    • prefer uses the lab server over the internet pools from Ubuntu's default configuration. The pools stay as a fallback if the lab server is unreachable, for example when the computer is away from the lab network.

    The 192.168.1.201 line must start with ^*. The internet pools are listed below it with ^- (usable, not selected) or ^? (not reachable yet). Both are normal.

  4. Check the offset:

    chronyc tracking | grep -E "Reference ID|Stratum|System time"

    Expect Reference ID : C0A801C9 (192.168.1.201) and Stratum 3, one more than the server. System time is this computer's estimated offset from the server.

Clocks a few tens of milliseconds off when chrony is installed are corrected gradually, not stepped. On 2026-10-14, homebrew05 started 24 ms behind the server and was within 0.2 ms about a minute later, with no step in the chrony log (journalctl -u chrony), while its container kept running.

docs.title: The Indoor Lab
docs.text: The Indoor Lab does not use chrony. Nothing indoors needs it today, because the Bebops are the only indoor quadcopters. It should be used there in the future, when PX4 quadcopters with companion computers are bought for the Indoor Lab.

docs.title: Undo
docs.text: Undo the server last. Clients that still point at it fall back to the internet pools, but their clocks no longer share one reference.

docs.title: A Jetson or Ground Computer
docs.text:
Go back to Ubuntu's default systemd-timesyncd, which removes chrony:

sudo rm -f /etc/chrony/conf.d/lab-time-server.conf
sudo apt-get install -y systemd-timesyncd
timedatectl timesync-status

timesync-status should show a Server: line within a minute.

docs.title: The Discovery Server
docs.text:
1. Remove the server configuration and list the firewall rules:

    sudo rm -f /etc/chrony/conf.d/lan-server.conf
sudo ufw status numbered

  2. If the list has a rule for port 123, delete it by its number:

    sudo ufw delete <number>

  3. Go back to systemd-timesyncd:

    sudo apt-get install -y systemd-timesyncd
timedatectl timesync-status

docs.title: File Backup Server
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-21

At a glance

Connect to the Autonomy Park's shared TrueNAS file share (192 TB) from Linux, Windows, or macOS. You must be on the Park network or connected through ZeroTier.

This will allow you to access all of our shared Autonomy Park files in the TrueNAS file share which has 192 TB of storage.

Note

The tutorial below for Linux is for accessing the drive via the NFS protocol, while the Windows and macOS ones use SMB. Both access the same data.

docs.title: Preliminaries
docs.text: First, you must be connected to the Autonomy Park LAN by physically being at the park or connecting to it via ZeroTier.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
In terminal, run

mkdir /home/$USER/uflautonomypark
sudo mount -t nfs "192.168.1.32:/mnt/Autonomy Park/uflautonomypark" /home/$USER/uflautonomypark/

Then, to keep from re-mounting every time you reboot, run

sudo nano /etc/fstab

and add this at the end of the file

192.168.1.32:/mnt/Autonomy\040Park/uflautonomypark /home/$USER/uflautonomypark nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0

Save with Ctrl-S and exit with Ctrl-X. You may now transfer files to and from the NAS.

To unmount the drive when not in use, run

sudo umount /home/$USER/uflautonomypark

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Open any version of Powershell (not Command Prompt) and run the following command.

net use Q: \\192.168.1.32\uflautonomypark /user:TRUENAS\autonomypark $PASSWORD /persistent:yes

where the $PASSWORD must be given to you by an admin. You may now transfer files to and from the NAS.

Note

Do not try and manually add the SMB share drive manually through File Explorer. It is not possible.

To remove the virtual drive, right click on it in File Explorer and click "Disconnect".

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Open Finder. Select Network in the left sidebar. (If Network doesn't appear because you've customized Finder, go to your Mac's name under "Locations" and you'll find it there.) A folder called "truenas" will appear. Double click on it. It may take a moment to load, but you will soon see a folder called "uflautonomypark". This will connect you as a guest, but guest access will be disabled by default for security reasons so you will not be able to access anything yet. Click "Connect As." It may take a moment to load. Fill out the pop-out that appears as follows:

  • Connect As: Select Registered User.
  • Name: Enter TRUENAS\autonomypark.
  • Password: Enter the password. (Ask an admin.)
  • Remember this password in my keychain: Check this box.

Click "Connect." It may take a while to load. Double click on the "uflautonomypark" folder. You may now transfer files to and from the NAS.

Note

On macOS, this virtual drive connecting you to the NAS will unmount automatically every time you log out. You will have to go back to Finder and remount. If you saved your login, double clicking the folder will get you back. Of course, connect to ZeroTier first.

Note

On macOS, the virtual NAS drive folder will remain mounted even when you disconnect from ZeroTier, but, expectedly, you will not be able to access files. It's easy to get confused.

docs.title: Large File Transfers
docs.text: Be careful walking away from large file transfers. Sometimes, failures to complete a large file transfer (> 5GB) will not raise error messages. This is important especially if you have a lot of small files that cumulatively have a large size. Verify that the sizes and number of files of the copied data and your local copy match for important transfers!

docs.title: Networking Equipment
docs.text:
Draft. Copied from the Autonomy Park's UniFi device list on 2026-11-06. The physical locations are not documented yet. Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

The Autonomy Park's UniFi (Ubiquiti) switches, access points, and gateway, and how they connect. Includes how to read the UniFi device list.

All our networking equipment is Ubiquiti. It is managed in the UniFi network console (see Reserving a Static IP Address).

docs.text:
The Indoor Lab's Wi-Fi networks are NCRLab and NCRLab_5GHz. Its networking equipment is:

Type Notes USW Lite 19 PoE 192.168.1.150. A switch U7 Pro 192.168.1.18. A Wi-Fi access point Cloud Gateway Ultra The gateway. Its IP address is Unknown. It is not listed in the UniFi devices, so this is not confirmed

docs.title: How to Read the UniFi Device List
docs.text:
• Type: the model of the device. The U7 Pro Outdoor and the U6 Lite are Wi-Fi access points (the Wi-Fi radios). The USW devices are switches (the USW Pro 48 PoE has 48 ports and powers the access points over Ethernet, PoE). The UDM SE is the gateway: the router, a switch, and the UniFi controller in one box.
  • Name: the label we gave the device in UniFi.
  • Application: the UniFi application that manages the device. All of ours say Network.
  • Status: whether UniFi can reach the device. Ours say Online.
  • IP address: the device's address on the network.
  • Uplink: how the device connects upstream, and the speed of that link. GbE is gigabit Ethernet. SFP+ (10 GbE) is a 10 gigabit link through an SFP+ port.
  • Parent device: the device it is plugged into, and the port number on that device. The tree above is the parent devices drawn out.
  • Channels (access points only): the Wi-Fi channel and channel width each radio uses. The channel numbers 1, 6 and 11 are the 2.4 GHz radio. The larger numbers (40, 149, 157, 161) are the 5 GHz radio.

docs.title: Networking Setup (Indoor Lab)
docs.text:
Written by Max Gardenswartz, Brandon FallinUpdated 2026-11-10Indoor Lab

At a glance

The Indoor Lab network has no Internet, so every computer needs a special netplan file. Follow this page to set one up.

Everything on this page runs on a Linux computer.

Our lab's LAN is not connected to the Internet, so each computer needs a special netplan file such that all DNS traffic goes to UF but all robot traffic stays on our private LAN. Our LAN has a WiFi component. While it can be joined, this is only for robots (unless you have two WiFi cards somehow).

docs.title: Route DDS Traffic Through Robot Network
docs.text:
Note

Every user on the Indoor Lab computers must do this step. Otherwise your nodes will not work.

To get all ROS traffic to be routed through the robot network, download the super client configuration file and put it in your home folder.

Download the Indoor Lab Super Client Configuration

Do not edit the file, not even the spacing. The Autonomy Park has its own file.

Download the Autonomy Park Super Client Configuration

Lastly, set the following environment variables in .bashrc 

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=0
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_fastrtps_cpp
export FASTRTPS_DEFAULT_PROFILES_FILE=/home/$USERNAME@ad.ufl.edu/indoor-lab-superclient-config.xml
Open a new terminal and run your ROS nodes without any networking issues!

docs.title: Route DNS Traffic Through UF Network
docs.text:
Warning

ONLY PERFORM THE FOLLOWING STEPS IF YOU ARE SETTING UP THE COMPUTER OR SOMETHING WITH THE NETWORK IS BROKEN.

To make everything work properly, we use the following netplan file. Run sudo nano /etc/netplan/01-network-manager-all.yaml and paste the following. This example is for the computer under IP 192.168.1.202 (MAE-BPLJHL2).

You will need to know the device name for your Ethernet (used for robots/LAN) and wireless/WiFi adapater (all computers have a built-in card for it) from ifconfig.

Replace enp0s31f6 with your computer's unique Ethernet interface name. dhcp4: true lets the Ubiquiti router dictate the IP, which should be statically assigned in the Ubiquiti portal. The Ubiquiti router also tries to serve a DNS and default gateway with this local IP, so dhcp4-overrides disables them.

network:
  version: 2
  renderer: NetworkManager
  ethernets:
    enp0s31f6:
      dhcp4: true
      dhcp4-overrides:
        use-routes: false
        use-dns: false
After saving, run sudo netplan apply.

docs.title: NTRIP Caster for RTK on Quadcopters
NTRIP Caster for RTK on Quadcopters
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy Park

At a glance

How the Autonomy Park's local NTRIP caster is built from the Emlid RS3 and RTKLIB's str2str, so the quadcopters get RTK corrections over the network. Reference only: the caster is already running.

Reference Only

This page is for reference. The Autonomy Park's discovery computer (see IP Reservations) is already set up as the caster described below. You do not need to follow these steps to use RTK. To use RTK on a robot, see RTK Setup.

A Username and Password Are Required

The caster will not start without a username and password. Every command below that starts it has them in the stream path as <username>:<password>. Replace both with the real values, which are not on the wiki: see Contacts. Every client needs the same pair.

This is the setup that is running on the discovery computer (Ubuntu 22.04, RTKLIB str2str), written up with the fixes found along the way, a section on the required username and password, and a section for undoing everything. It was last written up on 2026-10-16.

docs.title: The Values Used
docs.text:
Replace these if the network changes.

Name Value Meaning RS3 address 192.168.1.13 The Emlid RS3 on the Wi-Fi network RS3 TCP port 9000 Port the RS3 listens on once its output is set to TCP, role Server Caster computer discovery (192.168.1.201) The Ubuntu 22.04 computer running str2str Caster port 2101 Port the robots connect to Mountpoint BASE The name of the stream in the URL. Any name works if every client uses the same one Service name ntrip-caster The systemd unit Service user rtk A system user with no login that owns the service and the logs Log directory /var/log/rtcm Raw RTCM3 recordings

docs.title: How It Fits Together
docs.text:
Emlid RS3 (192.168.1.13)            discovery (192.168.1.201)                 robots
  TCP server :9000  <-- connects --  str2str  -->  caster :2101 / BASE  -->  Freefly NTRIP client
  (raw RTCM3)                           |                                --> lordmicrostain ROS 2 client
                                        +--> /var/log/rtcm/*.rtcm3 (hourly files, size-capped)

The RS3 has one connection (to discovery) instead of one per robot. str2str passes the RTCM3 bytes through unchanged and fans them out to every client.

docs.title: What Has Been Verified
docs.text: Item How it was checked Result ntripc:// caster output exists in the Ubuntu 22.04 binary str2str -h \| grep ntripc on discovery Works. The Ubuntu man page does not list it, but the binary does RS3 TCP stream reaches the computer str2str status line on discovery RS3 connected, about 4.1 kbps Caster serves data locally and from another computer curl --http0.9 on discovery and on superman ICY 200 OK then RTCM3 frames (message types 1124 and 1006 seen) Service starts and records logs systemctl status, ls /var/log/rtcm on discovery Active, enabled at boot, log files growing 8 simultaneous clients Test run against upstream RTKLIB b34 with a fake RS3 All 8 received data Username and password Same test setup, curl -u See the username and password section Log pruning script, user creation and removal Same test setup Worked Hourly cron entry Not tested The test setup had no cron installed Freefly and lordmicrostain clients Not tested Still the real acceptance test Reboot and RS3 power-cycle recovery Not tested Hourly log rotation Expected from the source, not yet confirmed Look for a file like 20261016_0000.rtcm3

docs.title: Make the RS3 a Raw TCP Server
docs.text:
1. In Emlid Flow, open the base's correction output and choose TCP.
  2. Set the role to Server, address localhost, port 9000. These are the settings Emlid staff gave in a forum answer (forum thread). The official RS3 docs page for this screen could not be loaded, so go by what Flow shows.
  3. Choosing TCP replaces the NTRIP server output, so there is nothing separate to switch off.
  4. Give the RS3 a fixed address (for example a DHCP reservation).
  5. Emlid's docs say Reach receivers can broadcast on two output channels at once (Base output 1 and Base output 2), which could let the ground robots keep LoRa while the computer takes TCP. The page does not list which pairs work (Dual base output). Two TCP outputs need different ports.

Check that the RS3 is sending, from the computer. The first command checks that the port accepts a connection. The second prints the first bytes of the stream, and RTCM3 frames start with byte d3.

RS3_IP=192.168.1.13
nc -zv -w 3 $RS3_IP 9000
nc -w 3 $RS3_IP 9000 | head -c 64 | od -An -tx1

connection refused means the RS3's TCP output is not enabled yet. A timeout means the computer cannot reach the RS3.

docs.title: Install RTKLIB
docs.text:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install rtklib
apt policy rtklib
str2str -h 2>&1 | grep ntripc

Expect version 2.4.3.b34+dfsg-1 from apt policy, and an ntripc line from the grep. The package contains /usr/bin/str2str (file list). If the grep prints nothing, build from source:

git clone --depth 1 --branch rtklib_2.4.3 https://github.com/tomojitakasu/RTKLIB.git
cd RTKLIB/app/consapp/str2str/gcc && make
sudo install -m 755 str2str /usr/local/bin/str2str

Then use /usr/local/bin/str2str in the service file below.

docs.title: Run the Caster by Hand
docs.text:
str2str -in tcpcli://192.168.1.13:9000 -out ntripc://<username>:<password>@:2101/BASE
  • -in tcpcli://...: str2str connects to the RS3 as a TCP client.
  • -out ntripc://<username>:<password>@:2101/BASE: it listens on port 2101 and serves the mountpoint BASE. The username and password are required.
  • No #rtcm3 on any stream: bytes pass through untouched. Format conversion only happens when both the input and an output carry #format, and its default message list is 1004,1019, which would replace the RS3's messages.
  • Status line, every 5 seconds: the characters are input, then each output. E is an error, - is closed, W is waiting, and C is connected. [CWC--] means the RS3 is connected, the caster is waiting for clients, and the log file is open. [CCC--] appears when a client is connected.
  • The timestamps on that line are GPS time, 18 seconds ahead of UTC.
  • If the RS3 drops, str2str retries every 10 s by default.

Test it as a client would:

curl -s --http0.9 -m 3 -i http://localhost:2101/
curl -s --http0.9 -m 3 -u <username>:<password> -H "Ntrip-Version: Ntrip/2.0" http://localhost:2101/BASE | head -c 40 | od -c

The first command fetches the sourcetable and the second fetches the stream. Expect SOURCETABLE 200 OK with a bare STR;BASE; entry, then ICY 200 OK followed by byte 0xD3 (octal 323). The curl option --http0.9 is required because curl 8.5 refuses the caster's ICY 200 OK reply otherwise. The second command exits with code 28 (timeout) because the stream never ends.

Things learned in testing:

  • A client request without a User-Agent header gets an empty reply (the caster drops it).
  • The mountpoint is whatever follows the first / in the request path and must equal BASE exactly. A request for any other mountpoint returns the sourcetable instead of data.
  • Do not run this command by hand while the service is running. Both want port 2101, and the second one fails with stream server start error. Stop the service first with sudo systemctl stop ntrip-caster.

docs.title: Run It as a Service with Logging
docs.text:
sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin rtk
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/rtcm && sudo chown rtk /var/log/rtcm

Put this in /etc/systemd/system/ntrip-caster.service:

[Unit]
Description=RTKLIB NTRIP caster for Emlid RS3
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=rtk
ExecStart=/usr/bin/str2str -in tcpcli://192.168.1.13:9000 \
  -out ntripc://<username>:<password>@:2101/BASE \
  -out file:///var/log/rtcm/%%Y%%m%%d_%%h%%M.rtcm3::S=1
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Then start it and follow its log:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now ntrip-caster
journalctl -u ntrip-caster -f
  • %% in a unit file becomes a literal %. Log file names like 20261015_2343.rtcm3 show this works.
  • Log file names use UTC (GPS time), not local time. S=1 swaps files every hour.
  • If the service fails with stream server start error, one stream could not open. Reproduced causes are a busy port 2101 (sudo ss -ltnp | grep 2101) and a log directory the rtk user cannot write (sudo -u rtk touch /var/log/rtcm/write_test).

docs.title: Cap the Log Size
docs.text:
This script deletes the oldest closed RTCM logs until the directory is under a size limit. It never deletes the newest file, because that one is still being written. The size limit is in MB and defaults to 20480 (20 GB, an arbitrary choice; change it).

sudo tee /usr/local/bin/rtcm-prune.sh >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
DIR="${1:-/var/log/rtcm}"
MAX_MB="${2:-20480}"
MAX_BYTES=$((MAX_MB * 1024 * 1024))
while :; do
  total=$(find "$DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.rtcm3' -printf '%s\n' | awk '{s+=$1} END{print s+0}')
  [ "$total" -le "$MAX_BYTES" ] && break
  count=$(find "$DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.rtcm3' | wc -l)
  [ "$count" -le 1 ] && break
  oldest=$(find "$DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.rtcm3' -printf '%T@ %p\n' | sort -n | head -n1 | cut -d' ' -f2-)
  rm -f -- "$oldest"
done
EOF
sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/rtcm-prune.sh

Test it on throwaway files before trusting it with real logs. Expect f3, f4 and f5 to be left.

mkdir /tmp/prunetest && for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do head -c 1048576 /dev/zero > /tmp/prunetest/f$i.rtcm3; touch -d "2026-10-1$i 00:00" /tmp/prunetest/f$i.rtcm3; done
/usr/local/bin/rtcm-prune.sh /tmp/prunetest 3 && ls /tmp/prunetest
rm -r /tmp/prunetest

Run it hourly. The first command checks that both succeed (the hourly folder exists and cron is active).

ls -d /etc/cron.hourly && systemctl is-active cron
printf '#!/bin/sh\n/usr/local/bin/rtcm-prune.sh /var/log/rtcm 20480\n' | sudo tee /etc/cron.hourly/rtcm-prune >/dev/null
sudo chmod 755 /etc/cron.hourly/rtcm-prune
sudo /etc/cron.hourly/rtcm-prune && echo "ran OK"

docs.title: Configure the Clients
docs.text:
Both clients take host 192.168.1.201, port 2101, and mountpoint BASE.

  • Freefly: fill in the username and password fields.
  • lordmicrostain ROS 2 client: set authenticate to true and fill in username and password. The README says both must be supplied in that case (README).
  • dotenv file: use NTRIP_MOUNTPOINT=BASE with no leading slash.
  • ntrip_version: the README does not list accepted values. Keep whatever your template uses for version 2. The caster does not check that header.
  • If a client shows no data, check the caster's status line: the second character should change from W to C when a client connects. Common causes are a missing User-Agent header, a wrong mountpoint, or a client that rejects the ICY 200 OK reply. None of these has been observed with the real clients yet.

docs.title: The Username and Password
docs.text:
The caster needs one username and one password for the mountpoint, and it will not start without them. In the stream path the format is ntripc://<username>:<password>@:2101/BASE. This was tested against upstream RTKLIB b34 with curl:

Request Result No credentials, correct mountpoint HTTP/1.0 401 Unauthorized Right username, wrong password HTTP/1.0 401 Unauthorized Wrong username, right password HTTP/1.0 401 Unauthorized Correct credentials ICY 200 OK followed by RTCM3 data

docs.title: Set or Change Them
docs.text:
1. Pick a username and a password. Use letters and digits only. Special characters were not tested, and the stream path is split on @, : and /.

  2. Edit the service file and change the caster line, replacing <username> and <password> with yours:

    -out ntripc://<username>:<password>@:2101/BASE \

  3. Apply it and test. The first curl should print HTTP/1.0 401 Unauthorized. The second should print ICY 200 OK.

    sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart ntrip-caster
curl -s --http0.9 -m 3 -i http://localhost:2101/BASE | head -c 60
curl -s --http0.9 -m 3 -u <username>:<password> http://localhost:2101/BASE | head -c 12 | od -c

  4. Update every client at the same moment, or the ones you did not update will be refused.

docs.title: What This Does and Does Not Protect
docs.text:
• The username and password are visible to anyone who can run ps on discovery, and in systemctl status. In the test, ps showed the full command line including the password.
  • The sourcetable (curl http://localhost:2101/) is still served without credentials. The caster checks the mountpoint before it checks the password.
  • HTTP Basic authentication sends the credentials without encryption (they are only base64-encoded). That is fine for a lab network and not for the open Internet.
  • The password stops other devices from pulling the stream. Anyone on the network can still see that the caster exists and which mountpoint it serves, because of the open sourcetable above.

docs.title: Undo Everything
docs.text: Work through these in order. The service must be stopped before its user and log directory are removed.

docs.title: Remove the Caster from the Computer
docs.text:
sudo systemctl disable --now ntrip-caster
sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/ntrip-caster.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm -f /etc/cron.hourly/rtcm-prune /usr/local/bin/rtcm-prune.sh
sudo rm -r /var/log/rtcm
sudo userdel rtk

rm -r /var/log/rtcm deletes all recorded RTCM logs, so copy any you want to keep first. userdel rtk removes the user and its same-named group.

Optional, only if nothing else on discovery uses RTKLIB. The second command is only needed if you built from source.

sudo apt remove rtklib
sudo rm -f /usr/local/bin/str2str

In testing, useradd -r created both a user and a group named rtk and no home directory, and userdel rtk removed the user and the group. The apt remove step was not tested.

docs.title: Check That It Is Gone
docs.text:
systemctl status ntrip-caster
sudo ss -ltnp | grep 2101
getent passwd rtk
ls /var/log/rtcm /usr/local/bin/rtcm-prune.sh /etc/cron.hourly/rtcm-prune

The first command should report that the unit could not be found. The second and third should print nothing. The last should say "No such file" for all three.

docs.title: Put the Rest Back the Way It Was
docs.text:
These are outside discovery and are not covered by the commands above:

  1. RS3: in Emlid Flow, set the base correction output back to the setting you used before (the RS3 as its own NTRIP server and caster), and disable the TCP output.
  2. Clients: point the Freefly and lordmicrostain clients back at the RS3's own NTRIP settings and remove 192.168.1.201 and BASE from their configuration.

This guide did not touch chrony, ROS discovery, or any firewall (the computer has none, so no port was opened), so there is nothing to undo there.

docs.title: Reserving a Static IP Address
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-06Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

How to give a device a fixed IP address, in the UniFi network console. The Autonomy Park and the Indoor Lab both have UniFi Wi-Fi systems.

Every device on the Autonomy Park and Indoor Lab networks should have a fixed IP address, listed on IP Reservations. Both labs have UniFi (Ubiquiti) Wi-Fi systems, managed in the UniFi network console. On each network, the router (gateway) login portal is at 192.168.1.1. To get access to it, see Contacts.

Netplan Is Indoor Lab Only

The Autonomy Park does not use netplan files. The Indoor Lab computers also need them: see Networking Setup (Indoor Lab).

Jetsons: Set the IP Before the Hostname

Set a Jetson's IP address before you change its hostname.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Log in to the UniFi network console.
  2. Go to Client Devices.
  3. Find the device whose IP address you want to fix, and select it.
  4. In the panel on the right, check Fixed IP Address.
  5. Enter a valid local IP address that is not already reserved. UniFi will show you a warning.
  6. Add the device to the reservation list for its lab, found through IP Reservations.

docs.title: ZeroTier VPN Install
docs.text:
Written by Max Gardenswartz, Jordan InsingerUpdated 2026-10-21Autonomy Park

At a glance

Install ZeroTier to reach the Autonomy Park's computers and robots remotely. You need it to use the file share and robots from off site.

We use ZeroTier to connect remotely to Autonomy Park assets (computers, robots, etc.). ZeroTier is one of the few VPN services that allows for multicast, which lets us publish and subscribe to ROS topics when we are not at the park. For example, we've done remote experiments with the AFRL Aviary before to demonstrate robustness to intermittent feedback and severe delays.

docs.title: Network ID
docs.text:
Navigate to the "ZeroTier" bookmark when signed in to Chrome as the Autonomy Park to find the 16-character Network ID. Do not share this ID.

Warning

If your local network uses the subnet 192.168.1.XXX you will run into IP conflicts. We are working on changing this.

docs.title: Windows and macOS
docs.text:
To install ZeroTier on Windows or macOS, go to the official download page at https://www.zerotier.com/download/ and download and install the client. After installation, the ZeroTier icon will appear in your system tray.

To connect to a network, right-click (Windows) or click (macOS) on the the system tray icon and select "Join New Network." Paste in the Network ID and click "Join." To confirm the connection, right-click (Windows) or click (macOS) the icon again. A checkmark will appear next to the Network ID, confirming a successful connection. To disconnect, click on the connected network item and select "Disconnect."

IMPORTANT: You must enable "Allow Default Route Override" and "Allow DNS Configuration". This will allow ZeroTier to redirect your network traffic through the ZeroTier network first rather than your default.

The two ZeroTier settings to enable.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
To install ZeroTier on Linux, run the following command in your terminal: 

curl -s https://install.zerotier.com | sudo bash

Once ZeroTier is installed, run systemctl status zerotier-one to ensure that ZeroTier is running. If it is not running, enter the command sudo systemctl start zerotier-one. Next, connect the Autonomy Park network. Run 

sudo zerotier-cli join $NETWORK
where $NETWORK is the placeholder for the Autonomy Park Network ID. It should return 200 join OK.

You are now connected to the Autonomy Park LAN. When you wish to connect/disconnect from ZeroTier, run sudo systemctl start zerotier-one or sudo systemctl stop zerotier-one, respectively.

docs.title: Authorizing Your Device
docs.text: Do not forget this step. After completing the installation steps, you should see the number of devices in the ZeroTier dashboard increase by one. Document the new computer you added by finding it, clicking "Edit", and filling out the Name and Description. Mark the checkbox next to "Authorized" at the top of the pop-up to allow access to the Autonomy Park LAN.

docs.title: Dog Startup Instructions
docs.text:
The commands run on your Linux computer, and then on the dog's Jetson.

  1. SSH into the dog's Jetson from your computer. The username and IP address are labeled on the side of the dog. Enter the password when asked.

    ssh <username>@<dog-ip-address>

  2. Run screen, so that the terminal is not killed if you disconnect. Press the space bar a few times until the text goes away.

    screen

  3. On the dog's Jetson, start the Docker container.

    ./openDockerDogsHumble.sh

  4. In the container, go to the localFiles folder and run the ROS 2 startup script.

    cd /home
./runUnitreeMinimalStartup.sh

When you are finished, press Ctrl+C to kill ROS. Then leave the container, kill the screen session with Ctrl+A then K, and confirm with Y. Then leave the SSH session.

exit

docs.title: Harness
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-21Indoor Lab

At a glance

A harness lets you test a low-level motor controller (for example, reinforcement learning) on a Go1 or B1 safely. No one has built one yet.

The harness frame holding a robot dog (from the Unitree Harness Manual).

The harness can be used with the Go1 or the B1 to test a low-level motor controller (for example, RL) on the dog in a safe way before having it work on its own.

docs.title: Autonomy
docs.text:
Written by Max Gardenswartz, Brandon FallinUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy Park

At a glance

How offboard control works on the Astros and its limits: the astro_mavros app, no SSH, no torque-level control.

Flying Manually has a tutorial video on flying the Astros and using autonomy with them.

MAVROS is needed for off-board control or teleoperation. See our astro_mavros app on GitHub.

Torque-Level Offboard Control Is Not Possible

On 2026-10-20 Freefly support confirmed that the Astros do not support the Micro XRCE-DDS Agent for offboard control, so torque-level control is not possible on them. Freefly has no plans to support it, even though AuterionOS does. Only Freefly can enable or disable it.

No SSH, and the App API Version

Only version 4 and newer of the Freefly app API allow SSH. Our stack, astro_mavros, uses version 1, so you cannot SSH into the Astros. Future Freefly releases may deprecate version 1. Freefly supports up to version 4, which would allow SSH, but this has not been tested. AuterionOS itself is at version 7 (App Framework), which Freefly does not support.

Topics Do Not Cross-Publish, but More Test Flights Are Needed

Freefly forces MAV_SYS_ID, which could make topics cross-publish into each other. astro_mavros is written to avoid this. More test flights are needed to be sure.

Software Versions

astro_mavros is tested with MAVROS 2.16.0 alongside the latest Freefly software. Astros running software older than 2.2.6 could no longer connect to the internet to serve topics, so they had to be updated.

The MAVROS pose rate of the Astros is 30 Hz and cannot be raised. (On the Homebrews it can.) The latency between the companion computer and PX4 is also rather high, and the Astros do not support uXRCE-DDS (see above). Use a Homebrew for controls experiments.
