docs.title: RC: Radio Control
docs.text:
These are the Taranis QX7 template needed to use the radio with this quadcopter.

Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason RC_CHAN_CNT 18 18 RC channels saved at RC calibration ❌ Default 0. Taranis QX7 template needed to use this radio with the quadcopter. RC_KILLSWITCH_TH 0.75 Kill switch threshold 0.75 ✅ Default 0.75. Fine as is. RC_MAP_ARM_SW 9 Arm switch on RC channel 9 ❌ Default 0 (unassigned). Taranis QX7 template needed to use this radio with the quadcopter. RC_MAP_AUX1 0 AUX1 unassigned ✅ Default 0 (unassigned). Channel 10 is the kill switch (RC_MAP_KILL_SW), so AUX1 must not also use it. RC_MAP_FLTMODE 5 Flight mode selection on RC channel 5 ❌ Default 0 (unassigned). Taranis QX7 template needed to use this radio with the quadcopter. RC_MAP_KILL_SW 10 Kill switch on RC channel 10 ❌ Default 0 (unassigned). Channel 10 is the right switch on the Taranis QX7. On main, kill zeroes the motor outputs immediately (mixer_module.cpp). Flipping the switch back within 5 seconds restarts the motors; after 5 seconds the vehicle disarms. That 5 s is hardcoded (COM_KILL_DISARM no longer exists, see the removed-parameters table). Be careful!!! RC_MAP_PITCH 2 Pitch on RC channel 2 ❌ Default 0 (unassigned). Taranis QX7 template needed to use this radio with the quadcopter. RC_MAP_ROLL 1 Roll on RC channel 1 ❌ Default 0 (unassigned). Taranis QX7 template needed to use this radio with the quadcopter. Taranis QX7 template needed to use this radio with the quadcopter.

docs.title: RTL: Return Mode
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason RTL_DESCEND_ALT 2 m 2 m (≈ 6.6 ft) ❌ MC default 10 m (metadata 30 m, overridden by rc.mc_defaults). The net is 8 m tall, so this keeps the vehicle clear of it. RTL_RETURN_ALT 2 m 2 m (≈ 6.6 ft) ❌ MC default 30 m (metadata 60 m, overridden by rc.mc_defaults). The net is 8 m tall, so this keeps the vehicle clear of it.

docs.title: SENS: Sensors
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason SENS_BOARD_ROT 2 Autopilot board rotated Yaw 90° ❌ Default 0 (no rotation). Required for how the CubePilot is placed in the case. Requires reboot. SENS_EN_PMW3901 0 Local PMW3901 optical flow driver disabled ✅ Default 0 (disabled). This enables a PMW3901 wired to the Cube's SPI bus. The optical flow sensor is on CAN instead (see UAVCAN_SUB_FLOW). SENS_EN_SF0X 8 LW20/c ❌ Default 1 (SF02). Selects the model of the serial LightWare lidar. It only appears when SENS_SF0X_CFG is not disabled, so it does not need to be set (and is not in the .params file). SENS_EN_SF1XX 6 SF/LW20/c ❌ Default 0 (disabled). The LW20/c on I2C is the only distance sensor used for estimation. Requires reboot. Options 8 (GRF250) and 9 (GRF500) are new on main; our value 6 is unchanged. SENS_FLOW_ROT 0 No rotation ✅ Default 0 (no rotation). Rotation of the optical flow sensor relative to the airframe. It seems to work fine at 0, but Max was not able to verify which direction the optical flow sensor faces. SENS_GNSS0_DELAY 110 ms GNSS 0 delay 110 ms ✅ Default 110 ms (range 0 to 300). Replaces EKF2_GPS_DELAY, which the migration copies to both SENS_GNSS0_DELAY and SENS_GNSS1_DELAY; only slot 0 is set here since there is no second receiver. The type changed from float to int32 with the rename. GNSS measurement delay relative to the IMU measurements. No motivation to change. SENS_GNSS0_OFFX 0.010 m GNSS antenna 0.010 m forward of CG ❌ Default 0.0. Measured antenna offset. Replaces EKF2_GPS_POS_X (named SENS_GPS0_OFFX on release/1.18). Slot matching: the offset slot is matched to the receiver by device ID (SENS_GNSS0_ID). When all ID slots are 0 it falls back to the uORB instance index, which the main description calls "only reliable for serial GPS"; the Here4 is DroneCAN. If no slot matches, the offsets stay zero (VehicleGPSPosition::findParamSlot). SENS_GNSS0_ID is the receiver's device ID, a per-drone value, so it is not in the template. Bench-check that the offsets reach vehicle_gnss.antenna_offset. SENS_GNSS0_OFFY 0.000 m GNSS antenna on centerline ✅ Default 0.0. Replaces EKF2_GPS_POS_Y. Same slot-matching caveat as SENS_GNSS0_OFFX. SENS_GNSS0_OFFZ 0.217 m GNSS antenna 0.217 m below CG (body Z points down) ❌ Default 0.0. Measured antenna offset. Replaces EKF2_GPS_POS_Z. Same slot-matching caveat as SENS_GNSS0_OFFX. SENS_IMU_MODE 0 Sensors hub does not select the primary IMU (needed for multi-EKF) ❌ Default 1 (publish primary IMU selection). Required by EKF2_MULTI_IMU = 3: the v1.16 description of EKF2_MULTI_IMU says "Requires SENS_IMU_MODE 0". Requires reboot. SENS_SF0X_CFG 0 Disabled ✅ Default 0 (disabled). Serial port configuration for the LightWare lidar (that is, UART). Since the LW20/c is on I2C (SENS_EN_SF1XX), this stays disabled to prevent PX4 from getting confused.

docs.title: SEP: Septentrio GPS
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason SEP_PORT1_CFG 0 Septentrio driver disabled ✅ Default 0 (disabled). The GPS is the Here4 on DroneCAN, so the Septentrio serial driver stays off.

docs.title: SER: Serial Ports
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason SER_TEL1_BAUD 57600 TELEM 1 at 57600 baud ✅ Default 57600. The QGC telemetry radio on TELEM 1 (MAV_0_CONFIG); the radio must use the same baud rate. Requires reboot. SER_TEL2_BAUD 921600 TELEM 2 at 921600 baud ✅ Default 921600. The Jetson link on TELEM 2 (MAV_1_CONFIG). Requires reboot.

docs.title: SF1XX: LightWare Lidar (I2C)
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason SF1XX_MODE 1 Enabled ✅ Default 1 (enabled). Operation mode of the LightWare lidar driver. The other option, 2 (disabled during VTOL fast forward flight), is for VTOL vehicles and is not relevant here.

docs.title: SYS: System
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason SYS_AUTOSTART 4001 Generic Quadcopter (airframe 4001_quad_x) ❌ Default 0 (none). Uses the multicopter for PX4 default parameters. Requires reboot. SYS_HAS_BARO 1 Barometer expected ✅ Default 1 (on). Pre-flight check for a barometer; if disabled, the preflight checks do not look for one. Requires reboot. SYS_HAS_GPS 1 GPS expected ✅ Default 1 (on). Controls whether the vehicle has a GPS. If disabled, the sensors hub does not process sensor_gps at all and GPS is not available to the rest of the system, so this must stay on. Requires reboot. SYS_HAS_MAG 1 One magnetometer expected ✅ Default 1 (on). Number of magnetometers the pre-flight check requires: 0 means none is expected, and 1 to N require N magnetometers to be present. Requires reboot. SYS_HAS_NUM_DIST 1 One distance sensor required ❌ Default 0 (check disabled). The preflight check fails if fewer than this number of distance sensors with valid data are present. Set to 1 so that a missing or silent LW20/c is caught before flight. SYS_HAS_NUM_OF 1 One optical flow sensor required ❌ Default 0 (check disabled). The preflight check fails if fewer than this number of optical flow sensors with valid data are present (the maximum is 1). Set to 1 so that a missing or silent flow sensor is caught before flight. SYS_USB_AUTO 2 MAVLink starts on USB right away ✅ Default 2 (MAVLink). Per the PX4 serial configuration documentation, it selects whether the USB port runs no particular protocol, auto-detects the protocol, or is set to MAVLink. With MAVLink, PX4 starts MAVLink on USB as soon as USB is available instead of waiting to receive data first. Keep it at default so the USB link works right away.

docs.title: THR: Thrust Model
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason THR_MDL_FAC 0.3 Thrust model factor 0.3 (30% quadratic term) ❌ Default 0. Usually determined by a bench thrust test. This value is a good guess that works in flight, so there is no motivation to change it.

docs.title: UAVCAN: DroneCAN
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason UAVCAN_ENABLE 2 Sensors, automatic config ❌ Default 0 (disabled). DroneCAN must be on for the Here4 and the flow/rangefinder node. Value 2 allocates node IDs dynamically. Requires reboot. UAVCAN_PUB_RTCM 1 Publish RTCM stream ❌ Default 0. Required for PX4 to accept RTK corrections over DroneCAN. Requires reboot. UAVCAN_RNG_MAX 100 m Rangefinder maximum range 100 m ❌ Default 999 m. The maximum valid range accepted from a rangefinder connected over DroneCAN. 100 m is the rated maximum range of the LW20/c. As far as I can tell from the description, it only applies to a DroneCAN rangefinder (UAVCAN_SUB_RNG, which is 0 here) and not to the LW20/c on I2C. UAVCAN_RNG_MIN 0 m Rangefinder minimum range 0 m ✅ Default 0 m. The minimum valid range accepted from a rangefinder connected over DroneCAN. Technically the rated minimum for the LW20/c is 0.2 m, but this works so it is fine. The same caveat as for UAVCAN_RNG_MAX applies. UAVCAN_SUB_FLOW 1 Optical flow subscription enabled ❌ Default 0. The optical flow sensor is on the CAN bus. This subscribes to its flow data only; its distance sensor is controlled separately by UAVCAN_SUB_RNG. Requires reboot. UAVCAN_SUB_GPS 1 GPS subscription enabled ✅ Default 1. The Here4 provides GPS over DroneCAN. Requires reboot. UAVCAN_SUB_IMU 0 IMU subscription disabled ✅ Default 0. No external IMU on CAN; the IMUs are inside the Cube. Requires reboot. UAVCAN_SUB_MAG 1 Magnetometer subscription enabled ✅ Default 1. The Here4 provides a compass over DroneCAN. Max is not sure this compass is actually the one being used (see EKF2_MULTI_MAG). Requires reboot. UAVCAN_SUB_RNG 0 Range finder subscription disabled ✅ Default 0. The only distance sensor is the LW20/c on I2C. The optical flow sensor's own distance sensor must never be used for estimation. Requires reboot.

docs.title: USB: USB MAVLink
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason USB_MAV_MODE 2 Onboard message set on USB ✅ Default 2 (Onboard). The MAVLink profile used on the USB port when MAVLink is set or detected (SYS_USB_AUTO). The PX4 documentation says the USB port is by default a MAVLink port with the onboard profile meant for companion computers, the same message set as MAV_1_MODE.

docs.title: uXRCE: A MAVROS Alternative
docs.text: Parameter Name Setting (Raw) Setting (Word) Is Default (MC) Reason UXRCE_DDS_CFG 0 Disabled ✅ Default 0. Turns on the UXRCE-DDS Client (alternative to MAVROS that allows torque-level control but foregoes RTK on main; PR #29368 adds an RTCM input topic, see MAV_0_CONFIG). UXRCE_DDS_DOM_ID 0 ROS Domain ID ✅ Default 0. Must match ROS setup. UXRCE_DDS_PTCFG 2 Custom participant ❌ Default 0. Required if using discovery server. Needs a XML config and file on fs/microsd/etc/. This parameter only appears if UXRCE_DDS_CFG is not zero. Ignore if not using uXCRE.

docs.title: Removed or renamed since v1.16.2
docs.text:
Every name below was in the 1.16.2 template and does not exist on main. Verified by running the PX4 parameter metadata generator on both source trees.

1.16.2 parameter (value) On main What it means EKF2_GPS_POS_X / Y / Z (0.01 / 0 / 0.217) SENS_GNSS0_OFFX / Y / Z Renamed twice (SENS_GPS0_* on release/1.18). Migrated automatically on import. EKF2_GPS_DELAY (110) SENS_GNSS0_DELAY, SENS_GNSS1_DELAY Renamed; copied to both slots; float became int32. EKF2_GPS_CHECK (1023) GNSS_CHECK (2047) Renamed, but the carried value would leave the new fix-type bit off; set explicitly. EKF2_REQ_EPH / EPV / HDRIFT / NSATS / PDOP / SACC / VDRIFT GNSS_REQ_* Renamed, same defaults. MPC_LAND_RC_HELP (0) MPC_AUTO_NUDGING bit 1 A nonzero value migrates; 0 does not. COM_RC_OVERRIDE (3), COM_RC_STICK_OV (30) MAN_OVERRIDE_SPD Only COM_RC_OVERRIDE = 0 migrates (to -1); 3 is dropped silently. Different unit (stick travel per second). FD_ACT_MOT_C2T, FD_ACT_MOT_THR, FD_ACT_MOT_TOUT MOTFAIL_C2T, MOTFAIL_OFF, MOTFAIL_TIME Replaced, no migration, different defaults and units. COM_KILL_DISARM (0 s) hardcoded 5 s Removed by PR #26736 (commit 6b5147110b, 2026-03-14, "remove needless parameter"). Kill still zeroes the motors immediately, but the vehicle now stays armed for 5 s, and flipping the switch back within that time restarts the motors. With 0 the disarm was immediate and the kill could not be undone. COM_ARM_SDCARD (2) hardcoded warning A missing SD card never blocks arming now (sdcardCheck.cpp uses NavModes::None). The "no SD prevents arming" setting is lost. COM_POSCTL_NAVL (1) none Removed in 1.17.0. Position mode falls back to Altitude, then Stabilized, never to Land. COM_DISARM_MAN (1), COM_TAKEOFF_ACT (0), COM_OBC_LOSS_T (5), COM_IMB_PROP_ACT (0) hardcoded Our 1.16.2 values equal the new hardcoded behavior, so nothing is lost. BAT2_I_CHANNEL (-1) none Removed together with BAT1_I_CHANNEL.

docs.title: Case Study: Lidar and CAN Sensor Burnout
Case Study: Lidar and CAN Sensor Burnout
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy Park

At a glance

Lidars wired any way except the included connector on I2C 2 slowly burn out other sensors on the CAN bus, and a lidar that is already failing can damage the next drone it is plugged into. This is how the problem was found.

Never Power On a Wrongly Wired Lidar

Never power on a lidar that is wired with the custom connector instead of the cable included in the box. Doing so slowly burns out the lidar over time.

Lidars 02, 03, and 04 are likely burned out. They no longer have their original cables, so they cannot be tested. Whether the original cables can be soldered back without further intermittent issues is unknown. We recommend never plugging them in again.

docs.title: The Symptom
docs.text:
During bench tests on 2026-05-01 on Homebrew 08, the lidar reading (helps with height estimation) flickered rapidly between a sensible value and 0 on MAVLink Inspector (a page on QGC). The lidar was plugged into the flight controller (FC) via the CAN Extender using a custom-soldered connector. Whenever the battery was disconnected (thus power was given by USB only), flickering stopped. Readings reacted normally to changes in distance to ground.

Upgrading software and different drones with the same parameters exhibited the same behavior.

The two photos below show the same area of a Homebrew. The circled parts are the lidar wiring.

Incorrect: the lidar is wired with a custom-soldered connector. Never power it on.

Correct: the lidar's included cable on its adapter board.

docs.title: The Homebrew 05 Crash
docs.text:
On 2026-01-31, Homebrew 05 crashed during a manual flight in Position Mode. It drifted massively without any command and moved in a random "toilet bowling" pattern. This was all later traced to the custom connector on the lidar, used instead of the included one.

Homebrew 05 crash, 2026-01-31: manual flight in Position Mode with uncommanded drift and toilet bowling.

docs.title: What Was Found Later
docs.text:
• The flicker happens because two distance sensors are on the same CAN bus. The optical flow sensor has a distance sensor too. When the battery was connected, optical flow could then publish over the CAN, which clashed with the readers of the lidar due to the lidar's incorrect wiring.
  • The optical flow sensor and the distance sensor are very close to each other on the drone, making it difficult to test which sensor PX4 was using. PX4 auto-selects a new distance sensor if data is stale or invalid for more than 1.0 second.
  • Cutting and re-terminating the lidar cable (as half the Homebrews have!), or otherwise using anything but the included lidar connector, slowly burns out the lidar and other CAN sensors over time like the optical flow sensor.
  • The fix is to connect the lidar with its included cable and using I2C 2, not the CAN extender.

According to the PX4 logs, the lidar and optical flow on Homebrew 03 failed before its crash on 2026-10-09. As of its successful offboard flight on 2026-10-07, both sensors were working. While investigating, a lidar from a bad setup was found to damage other quadcopters whose lidar was failing or had already failed when it was connected to them. Whether the damaged sensors are recoverable is unknown and has not been investigated. The lidar units cost $400 apiece, so this is a good long-term task. However, since Max got RTK working on the Homebrews, optical flow and lidar are actually unnecessary and actually (very) slightly make PX4's setpoint tracking and ability to hold in Position Mode slightly worse!

docs.title: What to Do
docs.text:
• Use I2C 2 and the lidar's included cable. Do not cut the cable.
  • Do not move a lidar from a drone with bad wiring to another drone. It can burn out other sensors on the CAN like the optical flow sensor.
  • The status of whether each Homebrew's lidar is wired correctly or not is given in Known Issues.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Case Study: The Homebrew 03 Crash From a Saturated MAVROS Link

docs.title: Case Study: MAVROS Link Saturation
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy Park

At a glance

On 2026-10-09, Homebrew 03 flew into the net because MAVROS saturated the serial link to the flight controller and offboard control acted on old state data. Read this before you run offboard code of any kind on a Homebrew.

docs.title: What Happened
docs.text:
On 2026-10-09, Homebrew 03 crashed into the net. The same drone, parameters, and code had worked on 2026-10-07.

The round-trip time (RTT) on the data link between the Jetson and the flight controller was 2500 ms. Offboard control therefore acted on old state data. It believed the quadcopter was stuck on the ground, and did exactly what it should do in that case with that data: it launched the quadcopter into the net. Nothing in the offboard control code Max wrote was monitoring for this kind of failure.

The drone took off as part of an offboard program for Max's research. Instead of climbing normally, it launched itself straight upward into the net.

Homebrew 03 crash, 2026-10-09: the offboard takeoff launches the drone straight up into the net.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: The serial link out of PX4 carries only 40 to 64 KB/s. With all the MAVROS plugins on (which is the default, shockingly!) MAVROS requested so much data that the link saturated. PX4 never cleared the backlog of requests from MAVROS, so everything it sent back was late.

docs.title: What to Do
docs.text:
• Do not run MAVROS with every plugin enabled on a Homebrew. The latest version of homebrew_docker has the fixes to use fewer plugins. It also has the list of plugins deemed necessary for basic offboard functionality and safety checks.
  • Monitor the link while the offboard program runs. The example code in autonomy_park_sitl has a comprehensive set of tests needed to safely monitor this connection (and many other things) so the offboard program acts in a safe manner.
  • Control barrier functions for offboard control do not exist yet. They still need to be written, as of writing this.

homebrew_docker autonomy_park_sitl

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The Homebrew 02 flight controller has slow XRCE topics (94 Hz); the cause is unknown. See Known Issues.
  • Case Study: Lidar and CAN Sensor Burnout: the lidar and optical flow on this drone had also failed before the crash.

docs.title: Case Study: Porting the Parameters to PX4 Main
Case Study: Porting the Parameters to PX4 Main
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-03Autonomy Park

At a glance

A worked example of porting the Homebrew parameter template from PX4 1.16.2 to PX4 main: the method, the kinds of changes you will meet, and the decisions made. Read it before upgrading the fleet.

Date: 2026-10-22. Max is flight-testing PR #29368 (RTCM corrections over uXRCE-DDS) on a real Homebrew quadcopter on a branch of PX4 main. The flights were a success, and the PR has since been merged. The feature is expected (likely) in PX4 1.19.0 as a stable feature.

Warning

Do not use this case study, or the files it produced, to port to 1.18.0 or any other stable release. What was tested is main as of 2026-10-22 (commit 5f429033bf, the 1.19 development line). main already differs from release/1.18, and it will differ from future stable releases. For example, GNSS_CHECK, GNSS_REQ_* and SENS_GNSS0_* exist only on main; release/1.18 still has EKF2_GPS_CHECK, EKF2_REQ_* and SENS_GPS0_*. The point of this document is the method and the kinds of decisions, not the answers. Whoever upgrades the fleet must regenerate everything against the release they actually target.

docs.title: What This Is For
docs.text:
Someone, one day, will upgrade PX4 on every Homebrew quadcopter. The upgrade tutorial (written separately) tells you what to click. It does not tell you what to put in the parameter template, because that depends on what changed between the two PX4 versions. This case study shows one complete example of that part, for the parameters only, so a future graduate student knows what the work looks like.

The outputs of such a port are three things:

  1. A new Example Parameters for PX4 Main: the reference with one row per parameter, why it has its value, and whether it is at the default.
  2. A matching example-parameters-px4-main.params: the file you apply in QGroundControl after the airframe defaults are loaded.
  3. A check of Calibration Parameters: the list of parameters that are unique to each drone. If any of those names changed, that sensor has to be recalibrated after the upgrade.

docs.title: What Max Did
docs.text:
Max used an AI assistant (Claude) as a research helper, with one rule: everything is verified against the PX4 source, nothing is guessed. The assistant was not trusted for what it remembered about PX4. It was used to do the reading and diffing quickly, and every claim had to point at a file.

What was fed in

  • Parameters: the 1.16.2 reference, 202 documented parameters.
  • homebrew-px4-v1.16.2.params: the 1.16.2 template of just parameters in the Parameters page.
  • Calibration Parameters: the per-drone parameters that should never save transfered between drones but need to be ported/preserved during an update

What was asked

These params are all what my quadcopter uses for PX4 1.16.2. I'm about to test something in the current mainline PX4 code. Which of these params have had their names changed or have been reworked? You must verify against source. Do not guess.

Then, after reading the findings, Max made a decision on each case (below) and asked for the new files.

docs.title: How the Comparison Against Source Was Done
docs.text:
This is the part to copy. Release notes and parameter descriptions were used only as leads.

  1. Pin the code. Check out each version you care about as its own git worktree: the tag you came from (v1.16.2), and the version you are going to (here main, plus v1.17.0 and release/1.18 to understand the history).
  2. Generate the parameter metadata from each tree. PX4 builds a parameters.json from the *.yaml / *.c parameter definitions (the metadata_parameters target in cmake/metadata.cmake). A full firmware build is not needed; the same generator scripts can be run directly (Tools/serial/generate_config.py, Tools/module_config/generate_params.py, src/lib/parameters/px_process_params.py). On 1.16.2 one extra argument was needed (--inject-xml src/lib/parameters/parameters_injected.xml).
  3. Diff the metadata. For every parameter in your list: does the name exist? Same type? Same default, min, max, units? Same enum values and bitmask bits? That one script answered "renamed or removed?" for all 202 parameters at once. Result: 176 names survive, 26 do not.
  4. Read the migration code. src/lib/parameters/param_translation.cpp (param_modify_on_import) is where PX4 renames old parameters automatically. Read it, do not assume. Check also where it is called from (see Renamed).
  5. Read what consumes the parameter. A changed default or a deleted parameter only matters through the code that uses it, for example Commander.cpp, sdcardCheck.cpp, battery.cpp, gnss_checks.cpp, mixer_module.cpp, ManualControl.cpp.
  6. Diff the layered defaults. The "Is Default" column in our document is not just the metadata default. It is the metadata default overridden by rc.board_defaults (Cube Orange), rc.mc_defaults and the airframe file 4001_quad_x. Compare those files across versions too. Here none of them changed for the parameters in our document.
  7. Validate the new template mechanically. A script checks every name in the new .params against the generated parameters.json of the target: it exists, the type matches, the value is inside min/max, enum values are legal. That check caught a real error (see "Renamed, and PX4 Migrates the Value").
  8. Only then judge. Each finding gets a decision from a human.

docs.title: The Cases
docs.text: Each case below is a kind of change you will meet again. The parameter names are just examples from this run.

docs.title: Renamed, and PX4 Migrates the Value
docs.text:
1.16.2 main Note EKF2_GPS_POS_X/Y/Z SENS_GNSS0_OFFX/Y/Z Renamed twice: SENS_GPS0_* on release/1.18, then SENS_GNSS0_* on main. EKF2_GPS_DELAY SENS_GNSS0_DELAY (and SENS_GNSS1_DELAY) The migration copies the value to both slots. EKF2_REQ_EPH/EPV/HDRIFT/NSATS/PDOP/SACC/VDRIFT GNSS_REQ_* Same defaults. MPC_LAND_RC_HELP bit 1 of MPC_AUTO_NUDGING Our value was 0, so nothing to carry.

What to learn:

  • Release notes do not give a full picture of parameter changes. Only some changes will be highlighted in the release notes. Many will not.
  • PX4 cannot migrate parameters for you. PX4 has some code (param_modify_on_import) to try and "upgrade" old parameters, but you cannot rely on this. Manual re-selection and porting of all parameter is required. PX4 will silently get rid of old parameter names!
  • The type can change with the name. EKF2_GPS_DELAY was a float (type 9 in the .params file); SENS_GNSS0_DELAY is an int32 (type 6). The mechanical validation in step 7 caught this.
  • A renamed parameter can have a new matching rule. In this case study's upgrade, it happens to be that the antenna offsets are now matched to the receiver by device ID (SENS_GNSS0_ID). With all IDs at 0 PX4 falls back to the uORB instance index, which the parameter description itself calls "only reliable for serial GPS". Our Here4 is DroneCAN. If no slot matches, the offsets silently stay zero.

docs.title: Renamed, but the Migrated Value Does Not Mean What You Want
docs.text:
EKF2_GPS_CHECK (1023) became GNSS_CHECK. The same 1023 would be carried over, but GNSS_CHECK has a new bit 10 (fix type) and a new bit 11 (jamming). With 1023, bit 10 is off, so the new GNSS_REQ_FIX would never be enforced (which we want to enforce since this was not possible to enforce in 1.16.2). The new template sets GNSS_CHECK = 2047 (the default) explicitly.

Lesson: when a bitmask is renamed, compare the bit list, not just the name.

docs.title: Removed Completely, Behavior Now Hardcoded
docs.text:
Removed What it did for us What is true on main COM_KILL_DISARM = 0 Disarm immediately after kill Hardcoded 5 s. See the deep dive below. COM_ARM_SDCARD = 2 No SD card blocks arming A missing SD card is only a warning. The setting is lost. COM_POSCTL_NAVL = 1 Land when position is lost in Position mode Removed in 1.17.0. Falls back to Altitude, then Stabilized, never Land. COM_DISARM_MAN, COM_TAKEOFF_ACT, COM_OBC_LOSS_T, COM_IMB_PROP_ACT Our values equal the new hardcoded behavior Nothing lost. BAT2_I_CHANNEL Default only Gone with BAT1_I_CHANNEL.

For every removed parameter ask two questions: is our value the same as what is now hardcoded (then nothing changes) and if not, what do we lose (then someone must decide). Max reviewed this list and accepted it, after considering COM_KILL_DISARM below.

COM_KILL_DISARM. It was the one that worried Max most. Kill still stops the motors immediately, but on main the vehicle no longer disarms at once: it stays armed for a hardcoded 5 s, and flipping the kill switch back in that time restarts the motors. The parameter was removed in PX4 PR #26736. An irreversible kill was wanted to minimize the consequences of reactivating a killed drone, but the new behavior is acceptable. Pilots must now remember that after landing on a kill, they cannot deactivate kill too quickly: if kill was set less than 5 seconds ago, the drone can take off again. Max verified the new kill-switch logic in the test flights.

docs.title: Replaced by a Differently Shaped Parameter, No Migration
docs.text:
• COM_RC_OVERRIDE (3: auto and offboard) and COM_RC_STICK_OV (30 %) became MAN_OVERRIDE_SPD. Only COM_RC_OVERRIDE = 0 migrates (to -1); our 3 would have been dropped silently. The unit changed from a 30 % displacement to stick travel per second (default 1.0), so the old "30" cannot be converted. In code (ManualControl.cpp, Commander::manualControlCheck()) any of the four sticks moving faster than the threshold, in auto or offboard mode on a multicopter, switches to Position mode.
  • FD_ACT_MOT_C2T, FD_ACT_MOT_THR, FD_ACT_MOT_TOUT became MOTFAIL_C2T, MOTFAIL_OFF, MOTFAIL_TIME. No migration, different defaults (the C2T default went from 2 to 35) and a different time unit. Our policy for these was "leave at default", so we use the new defaults.

docs.title: Same Name, New Default
docs.text:
Our reference documents "Is Default" for every row, and many rows said "left at the default". When the default moves, those rows move with it unless a human says otherwise.

Parameter 1.16.2 default main default Decision BAT1/2/3_V_CHARGED 4.05 V 4.2 V Accept 4.2 V (reasoning below). COM_FLTT_LOW_ACT 3 (Return) 1 (Warning) Accept the new default. FD_ACT_EN 1 0 Accept the new default. EKF2_MIN_RNG 0.1 m 0.01 m Already 0.01 m. Now equals the default (the 1.16.2 note, "expected to become the default", is confirmed). MAV_PROTO_VER 0 2 Already 2. Now equals the default.

Worked example: BAT1_V_CHARGED. The old 4.05 V was a workaround. The voltage is measured on a quadcopter drawing about 5 A, and sag makes a full 4.2 V cell read about 4.05 V. On main the default is 4.2 V and the description no longer advises setting it lower. What does that do to the safety-critical thresholds? battery.cpp interpolates linearly between V_EMPTY (3.6 V) and V_CHARGED, so the same fractional thresholds now correspond to higher voltages:

Threshold Fraction Voltage with 4.05 V Voltage with 4.2 V BAT_LOW_THR 0.35 3.76 V 3.81 V BAT_CRIT_THR 0.25 3.71 V 3.75 V BAT_EMERGEN_THR 0.15 3.67 V 3.69 V COM_ARM_BAT_MIN 0.50 3.83 V 3.90 V

Every warning and the arming limit now trip earlier, which is more conservative. Max accepted it and left all four fractions unchanged. Two more consumers of V_CHARGED were found while reading battery.cpp: the over-voltage "spike" fault threshold (cells × V_CHARGED × 1.05) and the battery scale used only when MC_BAT_SCALE_EN is on (default 0, not set).

docs.title: Same Name, Changed Meaning
docs.text: COM_RCL_EXCEPT = 7 is a bitmask. Bit 1 meant "Hold" in 1.16.2; on main it means "Auto modes" (Hold, Takeoff, Land, Return, Descend, Follow Target, Precland, Orbit), and bits 3 and 4 are new. The same value 7 now also ignores RC loss during Takeoff, Land and Return. The metadata diff does not flag this as a rename or a default change; only comparing the bit lists does. Max accepted the new meaning in anticipation of allowing multi-agent setups (in which requiring multiple RCs is not possible since we only have one).

docs.title: Cosmetic Changes and New Options
docs.text:
No action, but the description column in the reference was updated so it matches updated descriptions from main:

  • Relabelled options: BAT*_SOURCE ("Power Module / Analog"), COM_ARM_WO_GPS (1 is now "Allow arming (with warning)", 2 "Allow arming (no warning)"; our 0 still means deny), COM_FLTMODE* ("Position / Cruise"), COM_RC_IN_MODE ("Joystick" is now "MAVLink"), COM_PREARM_MODE.
  • New options: NAV_RCL_ACT 7, COM_LOW_BAT_ACT 4, SENS_EN_SF1XX 8 and 9, new COM_FLTMODE* values.
  • Widened behavior: COM_ARM_HFLT_CHK now also covers watchdog dump files.

COM_ARM_HFLT_CHK is also a lesson in keeping a workaround on purpose. We set it to 0 because a failed USB connection blocks arming. PX4 issue #29346 (hardfault of the USB MAVLink task after arming following a USB unplug) is open at the time of writing (2026-10-22) and, per Max, affects our board. It is filed against the Cube Orange+, and its author says it is fixed on main by PRs #28185 and #28197; that was not verified in source. So the parameter stays 0, and the reference links the issue so a later reader knows when to revisit it.

docs.title: New Parameters Worth a Decision
docs.text:
• GNSS_REQ_FIX (new, default 3). Value 6 means RTK fixed. Max chose 6: there is no reason to fly without RTK anymore ever since Max set it up to be plug-and-play. Before this, Max would just wait for RTK anyways before flying. The check fails when the reported fix type is below the setting (gnss_checks.cpp) and needs bit 10 of GNSS_CHECK (see "Renamed, but the Migrated Value Does Not Mean What You Want"). With COM_ARM_WO_GPS = 0, arming is denied unless the receiver reports RTK fixed. It is a strict check, which is decisive before arming. Once the strict checks have passed on the ground, the checks that decide while armed are the relaxed ones with fixed limits (3D fix, 50 m, 10 m/s), so losing RTK in flight does not trip it. Any offboard code the user writes should really land immediately on a fix type below 6, just like Max's offboard tests do.
  • EKF2_SENS_EN (new, default 8191 = all 13 sources on). Next section.
  • GNSS_REQ_TIME (new, 10 s): left at default. Not every new parameter needs a value in the template; it still has to be looked at.

docs.title: Interactions Between Your Own Decisions
docs.text:
This is where a human decision and the source can disagree.

Stick override versus nudging. Max first wanted both MAN_OVERRIDE_SPD at its default and MPC_AUTO_NUDGING = 3 (yaw and landing nudging), so that the RC could adjust yaw and landing in autonomous flight. The source says otherwise: the MPC_AUTO_NUDGING description requires MAN_OVERRIDE_SPD = -1, and manualControlCheck() has no exception for nudging. With both on, only slow stick movements nudge, and a fast one switches to Position mode. Max decided that stick override is far more important, so MPC_AUTO_NUDGING stays 0. The two are effectively mutually exclusive, which was not visible from the parameter names.

EKF2_SENS_EN against the *_CTRL parameters. Each fusion source runs only if its EKF2_SENS_EN bit and its own control parameter are both nonzero (intended() = enabled && available; available comes from EKF2_GPS_CTRL, EKF2_OF_CTRL, EKF2_RNG_CTRL, EKF2_BARO_CTRL, EKF2_MAG_TYPE). EKF2_SENS_EN is applied only while disarmed. Max's bit choices:

Bit Source Set Why 0 GNSS 0 1 The Here4. 1 GNSS 1 0 There is no second GPS. 2 Optical flow 1 Must match EKF2_OF_CTRL = 1. 3 External vision 0 RTK is good; no mocap. 4 to 7 Aux global position 0 to 3 0 None fitted. 8 Barometer 1 Height estimate. 9 Range finder 1 Must match EKF2_RNG_CTRL = 1 or 2. 10 Magnetometer 1 Critical. 11 Airspeed 0 Quadcopter. 12 Ranging beacon 0 None.

Max's doubt, kept on purpose. Max was unsure how this has to match EKF2_OF_CTRL and EKF2_RNG_CTRL, and whether turning GNSS 1 off could stop the GPS from loading. The source answers the first (it is an AND), but not how it behaves on the vehicle. Being unsure is fine and expected; that is what a test flight, and an in-person check that the GPS still loads, are for. Write the doubt down in the reference, as was done here.

A human error caught in review. Max's first draft computed the value as 1798 from the binary string 0011100000110. Read with bit 0 on the right, that string has bit 0 clear and bit 1 set: GNSS 0 off, GNSS 1 on, the opposite of the bit list next to it. The bits listed (0, 2, 8, 9, 10) give 1 + 4 + 256 + 512 + 1024 = 1797 = 0011100000101. Always recompute a bitmask from the bit list and check it against the module.yaml/enum, not against the string.

docs.title: Things in the Old Reference That the Source Changed or Refuted
docs.text:
• The 1.16.2 note that EKF2_MIN_RNG "is expected to become the default in 1.18" was wrong about the version: it already was in 1.17.0.
  • The 1.16.2 note that RTK over uXRCE-DDS is impossible "because there is no topic for it yet" was true on 1.16.2, and was exactly what PR #29368 changed: it added /fmu/in/rtcm_corrections. That PR has since been merged after the test flights succeeded, so the sentence is now out of date for main, and for 1.19.0 when it is released (likely).
  • BAT3_I_OVERWRITE exists on main (it did not in 1.16.2).
  • The new MOTFAIL_* descriptions on main still refer to the old FD_ACT_* names. Upstream descriptions are not reliable either.
  • BAT_V_OFFS_CURR was in the 1.16.2 .params template but had no row and no reason in the 1.16.2 reference. It now has a row saying exactly that.

docs.title: The Calibration Parameters
docs.text:
Calibration Parameters lists what is unique to each drone. If a name there changed, the sensor must be recalibrated after the upgrade, because its saved value would no longer be read.

All 107 per-drone names were checked against main: CAL_GYRO*, CAL_ACC*, CAL_MAG* (offsets, scales, ODIAG, ID, PRIO, ROT), CAL_BARO*, SENS_BOARD_X/Y_OFF, RC1 to RC10 (MIN/TRIM/MAX), BAT1_V_DIV, BAT1_A_PER_V, LND_FLIGHT_T_HI/LO, COM_FLIGHT_UUID, EKF2_MAG_DECL. All names exist on both 1.16.2 and main, with the same type and default. The only change is that SENS_BOARD_X/Y/Z_OFF now have a range of ±45°, and the sample values are well inside it. No entry of Calibration Parameters needs to change for this port.

The test flight verified that the calibration parameters survived the upgrade: seemingly all of them carried over without being ported by hand. This is new as of the flights for PR #29368. One candidate addition is SENS_GNSS0_ID (see "Renamed, and PX4 Migrates the Value"), a new per-drone value.

docs.title: Decisions Max Made
docs.text: Question Decision MAN_OVERRIDE_SPD Keep the default (1.0). MPC_AUTO_NUDGING Keep 0. Override matters more (see "Interactions Between Your Own Decisions"). Removed parameters with hardcoded behavior Accepted, after the kill-switch investigation. GNSS_REQ_FIX 6, require RTK fixed. GNSS_CHECK set to 2047 so it is enforced. Renamed parameters Ported with their values. New defaults (BAT*_V_CHARGED, COM_FLTT_LOW_ACT, FD_ACT_EN, etc.) Accepted. "Is Default" column updated. Battery thresholds Unchanged fractions; the 4.2 V shift is more conservative and accepted. COM_ARM_HFLT_CHK Keep 0, link issue #29346 (open on 2026-10-22). EKF2_SENS_EN 1797, with the bit table above. Doubts recorded.

docs.title: What Was Produced
docs.text:
• example-parameters-px4-main.params: 194 parameters (the 1.16.2 file had 201). Every name, type and range validated against the metadata generated from main. Differences from the 1.16.2 template: 13 removed outright; 13 renamed (11 carried over with their values, one with a type change, plus GNSS_CHECK and MPC_AUTO_NUDGING, which get explicit values); GNSS_REQ_FIX, EKF2_SENS_EN, MAN_OVERRIDE_SPD and three MOTFAIL_* added; and five values moved to the new defaults (BAT1/2/3_V_CHARGED, COM_FLTT_LOW_ACT, FD_ACT_EN).
  • Example Parameters for PX4 Main: every row has its "Is Default" mark recomputed against the layered defaults of main (no mismatches), descriptions updated, a new GNSS section, a new MOTFAIL section, the EKF2_SENS_EN bit table, and a closing table of removed or renamed parameters.
  • Calibration Parameters: verified unchanged.

docs.title: What Was Tested, and What Is Left
docs.text:
• Firmware was built and the drone flew. The flight tests are described in PR #29368. Max also verified the new kill-switch logic.
  • Not recorded as verified: that SENS_GNSS0_OFFX/Y/Z reach vehicle_gnss.antenna_offset; that the estimator reports GNSS, flow, range, baro and mag as intended with EKF2_SENS_EN = 1797 (estimator_fusion_control); that the GPS still loads with GNSS 1 off; that arming is denied below RTK fixed; that issue #29346 still affects the vehicle.
  • The migration-path claim (see "Renamed, and PX4 Migrates the Value") and the claims about PRs #28185 and #28197 are inferences or hearsay, labelled as such.
  • main moves daily. The result is valid for commit 5f429033bf and the PR #29368 branch on 2026-10-22, and for nothing else.

docs.title: Checklist for the Next Person
docs.text:
1. Pin both versions as worktrees; generate parameters.json for each.
  2. Diff names, types, defaults, ranges, enums and bit lists for every documented parameter.
  3. Read the migration code and where it is called from.
  4. For each removed parameter: compare your value to the new hardcoded behavior; read the consumer.
  5. For each changed default: recompute everything that depends on it.
  6. Diff the layered defaults (board, airframe, rc.mc_defaults).
  7. Look at the new parameters in the groups you use (GNSS_*, EKF2_SENS_EN here); not every one needs a value.
  8. Make the human decisions explicit and write the doubts down.
  9. Validate the new template mechanically against the target's metadata.
  10. Check Calibration Parameters names the same way.
  11. Re-read every claim that came from a description or a release note, and either check it in code or label it unverified.

docs.title: Case Study: Position Mode Instability
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-03Autonomy Park

At a glance

In early 2026, Max was test flying all new Homebrews as they were built. 50% of Homebrews flew well in Stabilized mode but twitched, drifted, or crashed in Position mode randomly and intermittently (every third flight or every 10 minutes of flight time). This is what was tried and what changed after the 1.16.2 upgrade with lidar and optical flow enabled.

docs.title: The Pattern
docs.text:
Flight tests on 2026-01-16 and the months before on PX4 1.16.0 showed two kinds of Homebrew:

  • "Perfect drones": When flying in Position Mode, Homebrews 02, 07, and 09 held position with no movement when the sticks were centered (expected behavior), and also handled well in Stabilized mode. They were certified as ready for future autonomy experiments.
  • Homebrews that handled well in Stabilized mode but not in Position mode: Homebrew 04 twitched and crashed randomly one day, breaking the landing gear. Homebrew 08, 11 and 12 drifted, wandered up to 2 m, or twitched and crashed randomly one day.

Stabilized mode was always fine on every Homebrew, so the problem was in the position estimate or the position controller, not in the motors or the airframe.

docs.title: What Was Tried
docs.text:
Date Homebrew What was tried Result 2026-01-23 05 Set EKF2_MULTI_IMU to 1 from the usual 3. Position mode still performed badly. 2026-01-23 12 Reflashed the whole OS and rewrote all parameters. Perfect hover for 2 to 3 minutes, then aggressive drift and low-frequency oscillation, then a violent twitch that forced a crash landing from about 2 m. 2026-01-30 05 Flew repeatedly, with and without restarting. About every fourth flight was perfect. A front flip in Position mode broke the GPS antenna; the cause was a hard fault of unknown origin. 2026-01-30 08 Flew in Position mode with a bad fix. Twitched and crashed after 12 seconds. 2026-02-06 11 Tested the vibration hypothesis: remounted the canopy so it does not touch the flight controller, then recalibrated all sensors. Stabilized was fine. Altitude mode could not hold altitude, and Position mode could not hold position. It twitched a few seconds in and broke a landing gear while about 1 m off the ground.

On Homebrew 11, the PX4 log suggested a lidar problem: the lidar measurement was never used for anything. Vibration remained a concern. The task that followed was to replace the lidar.

Homebrew 03 and 06 on 2026-02-06 gave more clues. Neither climbed when flown over a hill, which suggests the height estimate was relying on the barometer only. Both also showed "height estimate unstable" errors on some (but not all) boots, and Homebrew 03 reported the distance sensor's bottom-valid flag as always 0.

docs.title: What Changed
docs.text:
On 2026-05-01 the fleet moved to PX4 1.16.2, and the parameters were changed to enable the lidar and optical flow (EKF2_RNG_CTRL=1 and EKF2_OF_CTRL=1). Earlier flights had been made without them enabled. Max simply wasn't aware of these sensors since he was new to these quadcopters.

After that, Homebrew 05, 08, and 13 flew as expected and were certified. Homebrew 13 flew three flights each in Stabilized, Altitude and Position modes, all as expected. No issues like the "twitching" and whatnot were ever experienced again.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
• A Homebrew that is perfect in Stabilized can still be bad in Position. Stabilized should be reserved for experience pilots but is a good debugging tool.
  • If not using RTK, GPS is not sufficient for stable flying on the Homebrews. It is, however, on the Astros presumably since the Astros have the benefit of a company-backed design and more expensivee sensors.
  • When the above test flights were run, no RTK corrections were used. With RTK, optical flow and lidar are actually not required and even make handling slightly worse. Max now recommends keeping them off. However, your offboard code must land if RTK fix falls below 6 (full fix) since there are no longer fallbacks! If flying manually, monitor QGC carefully for RTK faults (e.g., falling back to 5). Falling back from 6 (fix) to 5 (float) is not expected except after a crash.
  • Intermittent faults (perfect every fourth flight) are hard to debug. Save the log for each flight.

docs.title: Building PX4
docs.text:
Draft. Written from Max's notes. The commands are the standard PX4 ones. The macOS tab has not been run by the lab. Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-03Autonomy Park

At a glance

How to build PX4 firmware for the Homebrews, for any future version or to get an old one. The official guide is almost enough; this page fills the gap.

Build for the CubePilot Orange, Not the Orange+

The Homebrews use a CubePilot Blue H7, but the build target is the CubePilot Orange (cubepilot_cubeorange_default), not the Orange+. The Blue and the Orange run the same firmware.

This is how to make new firmware (or get an old version) for the Homebrews. Use it for every future PX4 version. To flash the latest stable release, you can use QGroundControl's Firmware tab instead (see PX4 Configuration).

The official guide is Building PX4. Follow it, with the one addition below: it is missing the step that runs the install script in the Tools folder.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Run these in a terminal on Ubuntu, in WSL, or on macOS. Native Windows is not supported.

  1. Clone PX4 with its submodules:

    git clone --recursive https://github.com/PX4/PX4-Autopilot.git

  2. Check out the version you want (e.g., 1.16.2) and update its submodules:

    cd PX4-Autopilot
git checkout <version-tag>
git submodule update --init --recursive

  3. Install the build tools with the install script in the Tools folder. This is the step the official guide does not mention:

    Linux / WSLmacOSWindows 
    bash ./Tools/setup/ubuntu.sh

    Restart your computer afterward, as the script asks.

    bash ./Tools/setup/macos.sh

    Building PX4 on native Windows is not supported here. Use WSL and follow the Linux / WSL tab.

  4. Build for the CubePilot Orange:

    make cubepilot_cubeorange_default

  5. The firmware is the .px4 file in the build/cubepilot_cubeorange_default/ folder. Flash it with QGroundControl's Firmware tab, as described in PX4 Configuration.

docs.title: Keep the Firmware
docs.text: Keep a copy of every .px4 file you use. The one for 1.16.2 is on PX4 Configuration.

docs.title: Service and Repair Manual
docs.text:
Written by Nicklaus Witham, Mingyuan (Damian) Gao, Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-21Autonomy Park

At a glance

How to repair common mechanical failures on a Homebrew, starting with the landing gear.

This page will serve as a service/repair manual for common Homebrew mechanical failures

docs.title: Landing Gear
docs.text: Identify whether the bottom horizontal rod or vertical rod connecting to the the bottom plate has failed

docs.title: Bottom Horizontal Landing Gear Rod
docs.text:
1. Use 1.5 mm screwdriver to disassemble inverted T shaped connector piece by removing the bottom screw.
  2. Remove the rubber stoppers from the end of the landing gear rod and pull the failed component through the T shaped connecter.
  3. Push the replacement bottom landing gear rod through the fixed T shaped connecter. Visually inspect to ensure rod is symmetrical and evenly spaced on both sides with respect to the connector.
  4. Re insert 1.5 mm screw into bottom slot of connector until translational and rotational movement of the new rod is restricted.
  5. Re attach rubber inserts onto both ends of the rod

docs.title: Updating Here4 GNSS Firmware
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-21Autonomy Park

At a glance

The only reliable method we found to update a Here4 GNSS module on a PX4 drone. For reference only: it made no difference for RTK.

For Reference Only: Do Not Do This Without a Reason

Max Gardenswartz did this once to see whether the updated firmware performed any differently with RTK than the stock Here4 firmware (version: Unknown) that is currently on every Homebrew. He found no difference. This guide is kept for reference only, and he hopes no one ever has to use it.

This guide walks through the only reliable method we found for updating firmware on a CubePilot Here4 RTK GNSS module (CAN node) when your flight controller normally runs PX4.

Read this whole document once before starting. The process is safe and repeatable if followed exactly, but skipping or reordering steps can leave the Here4 in an unusable (though recoverable) state.

docs.title: Why This Process Is Necessary
docs.text:
• You cannot use QGroundControl (QGC) to flash Here4 firmware. Period. QGC has no reliable CAN-node firmware-push tool for this device.
  • PX4 does support flashing CAN peripherals directly via an SD card (official PX4 docs) — but in practice, this gets the Here4 stuck mid-update. It is not unrecoverable, but it will leave your GPS non-functional until you complete the procedure below.
  • Mission Planner (the tool that does reliably flash this device) is built around ArduPilot, not PX4. Its DroneCAN detection does not work reliably against a PX4 flight controller — even with a known-good, freshly-purchased Here4 unit.
  • The practical fix: temporarily flash ArduPilot onto your flight controller, use Mission Planner to update the Here4, then flash PX4 back. The Here4's firmware lives entirely on its own separate microcontroller — flashing ArduPilot onto your flight controller does not touch the Here4 at all, it just changes who's "talking" to it on the CAN bus.
  • This tutorial may be relevant if the RTK setup you are using isn't working as expected.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A Windows computer. Mission Planner is stated to also work on Linux/Android, but in our testing it fails to connect on Linux even after the commonly suggested sudo apt install mono-complete fix. Don't waste your time on Linux — use Windows.
  • Mission Planner installed.
  • QGroundControl installed (you already have this for normal PX4 operation).
  • A CubePilot Blue flight controller (standard Cube carrier board).
  • A microUSB cable.
  • The quadcopter's battery must NOT be connected for the entire process below. Everything is powered via USB only.

Throughout this guide, "reboot" means: unplug the microUSB cable, wait a few seconds, then plug it back in. Do not connect the battery at any point during this procedure unless explicitly told to.

docs.title: Step 0: Back Up Your PX4 Parameters
docs.text: Before touching anything, export your current PX4 parameter file from QGC (Vehicle Setup → Parameters → Tools → Save to file). You'll need to reconfigure PX4's DroneCAN/GPS parameters from scratch after this process (ArduPilot and PX4 use completely separate parameter systems — nothing carries over automatically), and having your old values on hand makes that faster.

docs.title: Step 1: Check Your Wiring
docs.text:
The Here4 connects to the flight controller over CAN using a 3-wire (white/green/blue) cable — plug this into CAN 1 on the CubePilot Blue.

Ignore the red and black cable entirely. Leave it unplugged from everything for this whole process.

docs.title: Step 2: Flash ArduPilot onto the Flight Controller
docs.text:
Using QGC (while still connected to the quad as normal, over USB or your telemetry link):

  1. Go to the firmware flashing screen and select ArduCopter. The latest stable version is fine.
  2. Let it flash and reboot as prompted.

Your flight controller is now running ArduPilot instead of PX4. This is temporary — you'll flash PX4 back in the final step.

docs.title: Step 3: Set the Required ArduPilot CAN/GPS Parameters
docs.text:
Physical state at this point: quad powered via microUSB only, no battery connected, Here4 wired to CAN1 as in Step 1.

  1. Open Mission Planner and connect over USB (not radio/telemetry) — click Connect in the upper-right corner.
  2. In the parameter list, set the following:
Parameter Value CAN_D1_PROTOCOL 1 CAN_D2_PROTOCOL 1 CAN_P1_DRIVER 1 CAN_P2_DRIVER 1 GPS_TYPE 9 NTF_LED_TYPES 231 CAN_D1_UC_OPTION 1

CAN_D1_UC_OPTION is the critical, easy-to-miss step. The official Here4 manual (docs.cubepilot.org) does not mention it, but without it, the Here4 will not appear in Step 4 below.

  1. Click Write Params.
  2. Reboot the quad (unplug/replug the microUSB cable).
  3. Reconnect in Mission Planner and double-check every parameter above stuck. Mission Planner's parameter display is not always trustworthy immediately after a write — verify by reading them back after the reboot, not just trusting the write confirmation.

Important: After this reboot, CAN_D1_UC_OPTION will read back as 0 again. This is expected and correct — it means the CAN register did its job of resetting so ArduPilot can now see the Here4. Do not "fix" this back to 1; leave it as the post-reboot value shows.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm the Here4 Is Detected
docs.text:
Physical state: unchanged from Step 3 (USB only, no battery).

  1. In Mission Planner, go to Setup → Optional Hardware → DroneCAN/UAVCAN.
  2. Select the entry corresponding to CAN1. The Here4 manual calls this MAVLinkCAN1, but as of September 2026 Mission Planner has renamed this option — look for whichever entry corresponds to CAN1 rather than matching the exact old name.
  3. Click Connect — not the Connect button in the upper-right corner. This is a separate button in the top-middle of the DroneCAN/UAVCAN screen itself.

You should now see three entries appear: - org.missionplanner - org.ardupilot0 - org.com.cubepilot.here4

If you only see org.missionplanner and nothing else, stop and troubleshoot before proceeding — this means the Here4 isn't visible on the bus yet. Common causes: still running PX4 (Step 2 wasn't completed/saved), CAN_D1_UC_OPTION wasn't set before the reboot in Step 3, or a wiring issue from Step 1.

docs.title: Step 5: Get the Correct Firmware File
docs.text:
1. Go to github.com/CubePilot/GNSSPeriph-release/releases.
  2. Download the latest STABLE release — do not pick a pre-release.
  3. From that release, download the .bin file. Ignore any .apj or .elf files if present in the release assets — .bin is the correct format for flashing this CAN peripheral (.apj is used for flight-controller firmware, and .elf is a debug-symbols build for use with a hardware debug probe — neither applies here).

docs.title: Step 6: Flash the Here4
docs.text:
1. Back in Mission Planner's DroneCAN/UAVCAN screen (Step 4), find the org.com.cubepilot.here4 entry.
  2. Click Menu → Update.
  3. When asked whether to search the internet for the latest firmware, click No. In our testing, this internet search can return a mismatched or even older version specifically for the Here4 — always supply the file you downloaded directly from CubePilot's GitHub in Step 5 instead.
  4. When prompted, browse to and select the .bin file you downloaded.
  5. Let it run. Do not unplug the USB cable or interrupt this process.

docs.title: Reading the Here4's LED During This Step
docs.text:
This isn't documented well anywhere else, so pay attention to the LED on the Here4 itself while it updates:

  • Slowly pulsing white — normal. The update is in progress; let it finish.
  • Solid (steady, non-pulsing) white — this may indicate the update has failed or the unit is stuck in a bad state. If you see solid white rather than a pulse, stop and don't keep power-cycling repeatedly hoping it resolves on its own.

If the update genuinely stalls (no LED change, no progress) for an extended period — more than roughly 10 minutes with zero change — treat it as stuck rather than "still working," and move to the fallback below rather than continuing to wait indefinitely.

docs.title: Step 7: Verify the Update Succeeded
docs.text:
After Mission Planner reports the update as complete:

  1. In the DroneCAN/UAVCAN screen, refresh/reconnect and confirm the Here4's reported firmware version now matches the release you selected in Step 5.
  2. Confirm the LED has settled to its normal steady/breathing state (not pulsing, not solid white).

docs.title: Step 8: Return to PX4
docs.text:
The Here4 is now updated and independent of whatever the flight controller runs — but your quad still needs to fly on PX4.

  1. In QGC, flash PX4 back onto the flight controller (whatever version you were running before — we used v1.16.2).
  2. Let the flight controller boot on PX4's own default parameters first — do not immediately load your saved .params file from Step 0. Reflashing firmware families back and forth can leave the parameter set in an inconsistent state if you load a saved file over it too quickly. Let PX4 come up clean once, then load your saved parameters as a deliberate, separate step afterward.
  3. Re-set/verify your PX4 DroneCAN/GPS parameters. These do not carry over from ArduPilot. At minimum, revisit:
  4. UAVCAN_ENABLE
  5. UAVCAN_SUB_GPS
  6. UAVCAN_PUB_RTCM (if using RTK corrections)
  7. EKF2_GPS_CTRL

Use your Step 0 backup as a reference for the values you had before. 4. Confirm PX4 detects the Here4 again: open the MAVLink Console and run uavcan status — the Here4's node should show up with mode OPERAT.

docs.title: ⚠️ Double-Check Your Parameters Actually Loaded Correctly
docs.text: Do not trust a loaded .params file blindly — verify it, parameter by parameter, before you fly. In our case, after loading our saved parameters back in, several CA_ (control allocation / motor mixer) parameters silently came back wrong — for example, a value that should have been 0.25 loaded as 1.00 instead. We didn't catch this immediately, and it made the quad unflyable (the motor mixer was effectively miscalibrated). There was no obvious error or warning — the parameter file simply didn't apply cleanly across the reflash. Spot-check your critical parameters (especially anything under CA_) against your Step 0 backup after loading, rather than assuming the load succeeded just because it didn't throw an error.

docs.title: Recalibrate Your Sensors Before Flying
docs.text:
After all of the above, recalibrate the compass — this is required, not optional, after this process. In our case, one indoor calibration attempt wasn't enough to clear the errors; we had to calibrate the compass a second time outdoors before it stuck cleanly. If you see persistent compass-related errors after an indoor calibration, don't assume something else is broken — try again outside first.

For good measure, we also recalibrated Level Horizon, the accelerometer, and the gyroscope (i.e., all onboard sensors) at the same time, rather than just the compass alone. After doing all of this, the quad flew normally.

Only once you've verified your parameters, recalibrated all sensors, and confirmed a healthy GPS fix should you consider reconnecting the battery and proceeding to normal flight testing. You can put the GPS back on the CAN extender rather than CAN1.

docs.title: Fallback: If Mission Planner Still Won't Cooperate
docs.text:
If you hit a wall anywhere in the above — Mission Planner won't detect anything even after correctly following every step, or the Here4 ends up in the solid-white stuck state — the more robust (but slightly more involved) option is to bypass Mission Planner entirely:

  1. Buy a USB-to-CAN adapter (an adapter running "slcan" firmware, such as a CANable-style adapter, is a common and inexpensive choice).
  2. Wire the adapter's CAN-H/CAN-L leads directly onto the CAN bus, in parallel with the existing Here4-to-flight-controller wiring (CAN is a shared bus, so tapping in alongside the existing connection is fine).
  3. Install and run dronecan_gui_tool (free, cross-platform) pointed at that adapter.
  4. Flash the same .bin file from Step 5 through this tool instead of Mission Planner.

This talks to the CAN bus directly at the protocol level, with no dependency on either Mission Planner's or QGC's flakier CAN-over-MAVLink bridging — it's the method a PX4 core developer has used to resolve this exact class of issue in the past.

docs.title: Upgrading PX4 Firmware
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-22Autonomy Park

At a glance

Upgrading PX4 on a Homebrew is expert work. PX4 has no tool to port parameters between versions, so the template must be ported by hand and tested on one quadcopter first.

Updating PX4 Needs Serious Expertise

Do not upgrade PX4 on a quadcopter you plan to fly soon. Do it on a single quadcopter, as described below.

Case Study: Porting the Homebrew Parameters to PX4 Main What Is Safe to Upgrade

Upgrading May Get Easier

PX4 pull request #29363 introduces safe parameter migration from 1.17 to the 1.18 beta. Upgrading may be easier someday. For now, manual porting is the only safe way to upgrade from 1.16 to future versions.

docs.title: Why Upgrading Is Manual
docs.text:
PX4 does not provide a porting tool for parameters between versions. Major (1.x to 2.x) and minor (x.15 to x.16) updates often involve opaque changes to parameter names and EKF logic.

  • Standard Practice: Users are expected to reconfigure PX4 from scratch when a new minor/major version is released.
  • Legacy Data: If you update firmware from a previous version, PX4 will attempt to keep as many parameters as possible. This is undesirable and leads to errors.
  • Deltas: The comparison script, px4-param-diff.py, was used to identify differences between a working 1.15.4 set and a default 1.16.0 set to create our current template. Use it as a baseline for future upgrades (e.g., 1.16 to 1.17).

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Port the parameter template by hand. Go through Homebrew Parameters one parameter at a time against the parameter reference of the new PX4 version, and update the template for that version.

  2. Update PX4 on a single quadcopter.

  3. On that quadcopter, follow steps 2 to 9 of the Clean Configuration Procedure, then the battery voltage calibration in PX4 Configuration.

docs.title: Verifying the Upgrade
docs.text:
The biggest check is the parameter names: make sure every setting you want was ported to its new parameter name. (PX4 1.15.0 to 1.16.0 was a nightmare for this.) Stability of flight is not the main check.

Then fly. Do multiple manual test flights of about 60 seconds each, in Position Mode. Include at least one cold restart, by unplugging and re-plugging the battery.

Something is wrong if the quadcopter drifts in Position Mode with the sticks centered (see Position Mode Should Hold Position), if fix_type is ever less than 6, if flying feels off, or if the quadcopter crashes unexpectedly.

What a Good Fix Is for a Quadcopter

A good fix is fix_type 6, always. Read the fix_type entry of <namespace>/mavros/gpsstatus/gps1/raw. When everything works, every single message coming out of MAVROS shows 6 (RTK fixed) while flying around, never less.

This reliability is only tested up to three quadcopters under the current setup: RTKLib on the discovery server computer. Three agents have also been tested with the Emlid RS3's embedded caster, which sends corrections over an individual link to every quadcopter (every local NTRIP client). That is not reliable at all: the fix drops out randomly and intermittently. Even with one agent, flying can reduce the fix to 5 from what it was on the ground, with no recovery and no explanation. Use the RTKLib caster, never the embedded caster.

Wait for the Fix to Reach 6

Getting a fix takes 5 to 15 minutes. Until fix_type reaches 6, expect lots of "Global position estimate invalid" errors. A fix of 5 (RTK float) can make flights unstable, so it is very important to wait for 6 (fixed) before you fly.

The fix should drop to 5 or lower, even for a single frame, only if you hit the ground hard, crash, or the satellites cut out. (The satellites cut out once in 100 flight hours.) Moving fast or changing altitude should never demote the fix.

Multi-agent testing has not been done, so it is unknown whether network traffic, or changing access points, affects the fix.

An Easier Way to Check the Fix

Click the GPS icon in the Fly tab of AMC (Astros) or QGC (Homebrews) to check the RTK fix.

Position Mode Is Already Quite Fast

Be very careful. Move the sticks very slowly.

Never Upgrade the Fleet Before Test Flights on One Quadcopter

Upgrading the rest of the fleet without test flights on a single upgraded quadcopter first is a bad idea.

docs.title: Updating the Rest of the Fleet
docs.text:
Only after the single quadcopter passes its test flights, the person upgrading the fleet needs to:

  1. Save the firmware. Download the firmware for the CubePilot Orange from QGC's Firmware tab and save it to the wiki (see PX4 Configuration). It takes some digging to find the downloaded file. The exact steps: Not yet documented.
  2. Update the references. Update the Homebrew Parameters reference and the Calibration Parameters page, which are detailed on the PX4 Configuration page.
  3. Generate a new .params file like the current one in the parameter template. Do not generate it from a full parameter set saved from a working upgraded quadcopter: that set contains its calibration values.
  4. Apply the procedure in the Clean Configuration Procedure to every quadcopter.

When You Do Not Need to Wipe Parameters and Recalibrate

The Clean Configuration Procedure wipes all previous parameters (Reset all to firmware's defaults) and has every sensor recalibrated. You can avoid both if you verify that none of the calibration parameter names in Calibration Parameters changed in the new PX4 version.

If only some sensors had their calibration parameter names changed, a full reset is also not needed: recalibrate only those sensors.

If you cannot verify the names, the Clean Configuration Procedure must be followed in full for every quadcopter.

In that case, battery recalibration can also be skipped, because BAT1_V_DIV and BAT1_A_PER_V are calibration parameters too. Load the revised .params file (the same set of parameters, with updated names), reboot, and fly.

QGC May Show a \"Missing Parameters\" Message

After a firmware update, QGC may show a "Missing parameters" message. It can generally be ignored. It is common when updating firmware.

At a glance

Keep track of the hardware issues of the Bebops on this page and on Known Issues. See Edit the Wiki.

None of the cycle counts or ages of the LiPos for the Parrot Bebops are known. The following advice is generally given.

Note

Unfortunately, Parrot's proprietary chargers do not allow charging to storage voltages or even checking the battery voltage. This is why it's important to keep tabs on their swelling, as it's the primary sign of age.

docs.title: Connecting to WiFi
docs.text:
Written by Max Gardenswartz, Jordan InsingerUpdated 2026-11-10Indoor Lab

At a glance

For reference only: working Bebops are already on the Indoor Lab LAN. This tutorial sets a Bebop's Wi-Fi network and static IP address.

Everything on this page runs on a Linux computer.

For Reference Only

All working Bebops should already be connected to the Indoor Lab LAN. This tutorial is provided only for reference. Do not follow it unless a Bebop has lost its network settings.

Configure the network and IP on Bebop 2 drones and make changes persistent by adding them to the boot sequence.

docs.title: Step 1: Clone GitHub Repository and Edit shortpress_3.sh
Clone the Repository
docs.text: git clone https://github.com/tnaegeli/multiple_bebops.git

docs.title: Navigate to the Cloned Directory
docs.text: cd multiple_bebops

docs.title: Edit shortpress_3.sh to Set SSID, Password, and Static IP
docs.text:
• Open shortpress_3.sh in a text editor.
  • Modify the following variables. The Indoor Lab Wi-Fi name (SSID) is NCRLab (the 5 GHz network is NCRLab_5GHz). For the password, see Contacts.
SSID: 'NCRLab'
PW: 'Unknown'
IP: 192.168.1.1XX
  • The IP must be in the correct range—refer to IP Reservations.
  • After configuring, add the new IP to the reservations list.

docs.title: Step 2: Connect to the Bebop Using Android Debug Bridge (ADB)
Install adb (If Not Installed)
docs.text: sudo apt-get install android-tools-adb

docs.title: Connect adb to the Bebop
docs.text:
• Connect the Bebop to your computer via USB.
  • Power on the Bebop and wait for the LED to remain solid.
  • Press the power button four times until you hear the beeping sound.
  • Then run:
adb connect 192.168.43.1:9050
  • A successful message should read: connected to 192.168.43.1:9050

docs.title: Step 3: Run Script and Add to Boot
Run the File Copy Script
docs.text: ./copy_files.sh

docs.title: Open a Shell on the Bebop
docs.text: adb shell

docs.title: Edit the Boot File Using vim
docs.text:
vi /etc/init.d/rcS

To write to file, using vim type I to enter insert mode. To save and exit vim press escape to exit insert mode, then :wq to write to file and exit.

docs.title: Add This Line to the End of the rcS File Just Above the exit 0 Line.
docs.text: ./bin/onoffbutton/shortpress_3.sh

docs.title: Run ifconfig
docs.text:
Run the following code in the shell 

ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.1XX netmask 255.255.255.0 up
where 1XX is your desired IP.

docs.title: Exit the adb Shell
docs.text:
You're in a shell within a shell. Type 

exit
to get back to bash.

docs.title: Disconnect and Reboot the Bebop
docs.text:
adb disconnect

Unplug the USB and restart the drone.

docs.title: Assign Static IP to Bebop
docs.text: Now,the Bebop will show up on the TP-Link portal. Once the Bebop connects, log into the router and assign the IP reservation for the desired address under Advanced -> DHCP Server. Don't forget to add the IP to the Google Sheet! (see IP Reservations)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Ensure all Bebop IPs are unique and in the reserved range.
  • If adb isn't working, confirm the drone is powered on and connected via USB.
  • If you encounter file system permission issues, remount the filesystem as writable:
adb shell mount -o remount,rw /
ADB tends to not actually disconnect from devices even after running adb disconnect. You can force a disconnect using: adb kill-server.

docs.title: Firmware Update
docs.text:
Written by Max Gardenswartz, Brandon FallinUpdated 2026-11-09Indoor Lab

At a glance

For reference only: how to update a Bebop's firmware. There is no reason to update the Bebops; they all work as they are.

For Reference Only

There is no reason to update the Bebops' firmware. They should all work as they are. This page is provided only for reference.

docs.title: Download the Firmware
docs.text: The oldest version of the Bebop firmware that is supported by SDK version 3.1.4 is firmware 4.3.1. Download this version from the Bebop firmware folder.

docs.title: Connect to the Bebop
docs.text:
If not already installed, install the Android Debug Bridge tools by running

sudo apt-get install android-tools-adb

Connect the Bebop to the computer using micro USB. Press the power button on the back of the Bebop once and wait for the light to become solid. Then click the power button 4 times in rapid succession. You should hear a beep. Then, run the following in the terminal to establish connection:

adb connect 192.168.43.1:9050

After a successful connection, the CLI should say connected to 192.168.43.1:9050. Now, open a Bebop shell using adb.

adb shell

Tip

If you are upgrading the Bebop firmware from an older version, you do not need to modify the dgwl.txt file.

docs.title: Allow the Downgrade
docs.text:
Make the file system writable and open the whitelist of firmware versions that may be installed over the current one.

mount -o remount, rw / &&
vi /bin/updater/dgwl.txt

The file starts with a few comment lines, then a list of version patterns. The last two lines are:

0 \ .0 \ .0
3 \ .3 \. [0-9] \ +

Press i to enter text entry mode in vi. Add the version number of the firmware you downloaded as a new last line:

4.3.1

Press ESC to exit insert mode. Save the file and quit.

:wq

docs.title: Install the Firmware
docs.text:
On an Ubuntu computer, open Files. Click "Other Locations" and in the "Enter server address..." field, type ftp://192.168.43.1 and connect anonymously (No username and password). Rename the downloaded firmware to bebop2_update.plf. Copy the firmware file to /data/ftp/internal_000 folder of the Bebop. Go back to the adb shell and enter

/bin/updater/updater_scan.sh /data/ftp/internal_000

The Bebop prints the steps of the update. It should report that the downgrade is allowed by the whitelist, and then that it is sending the file to the Update partition.

Finally, reboot the Bebop by entering reboot in the adb shell. The Bebop will reboot multiple times for the firmware upgrade.
