docs.title: AI for Debugging Jetsons
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

How to give an AI coding agent such as Claude Code restricted, logged SSH access to a Jetson, so it can pull logs, add new logging, and speed up debugging on a quadcopter or any other Jetson.

Debugging a robot usually means hours of SSH, docker logs, copying files, and guessing what to log next. An AI coding agent running on your ground station can do much of that for you. Over SSH, it can pull logs from a Jetson, read them, add new logging to your code, run it again, and compare the results. This speeds up debugging on a quadcopter or any other Jetson.

This page sets up that access safely. The agent gets its own SSH key that can only run single commands (no interactive shell), and every command it runs is written to a log on the robot. You keep your normal password login.

The examples use Claude Code, but any agent that runs ssh commands works the same way. For the Jetsons themselves, see Jetsons.

Two terms are used throughout. The ground station is the computer where the agent runs. The robot is each Jetson. Every section says which one to run it on. Shell variables do not carry between computers or terminals, so each section sets the ones it needs.

Lockout Rules: Read All of Them Before Typing Anything

  1. Keep one working shell on each robot open the whole time. Open new terminals to test. Never close the working one until the tests pass.
  2. Confirm your human password login works before you restrict any key.
  3. Never overwrite authorized_keys (>). Only append (>>) and keep a backup.
  4. Never set PasswordAuthentication no unless you have another way in.
  5. Each authorized_keys entry must be one line. A line break silently breaks the key.
  6. If you lock yourself out anyway, see Recovery.

Props Off While an Agent Is Connected

While the agent is unlocked, it can run commands on the robot. Arbitrary shell access plus Docker is effectively root, because Docker group membership is root-equivalent. The safety layers that remain are the sudo password and props off and the ESC power disconnected during debugging.

docs.title: Create the Agent's Key (Ground Station, Once)
docs.text:
Choose the names. KEY_COMMENT is the label inside the key. It is how the key is found and removed later.

KEY_NAME=claude_robot_key
KEY_COMMENT=claude-robot-debug

Important

Set a passphrase when prompted. Do not leave it empty.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/$KEY_NAME -C "$KEY_COMMENT"

docs.title: Add SSH Aliases for One Robot (Ground Station)
docs.text:
Replace the three ROBOT_* values for the robot you are doing. The _claude alias uses the restricted key. The _me alias forces password login and ignores the agent.

ROBOT_ALIAS=homebrew02
ROBOT_IP=robot-ip-address
ROBOT_USER=robot-username

cat >> ~/.ssh/config <<EOF

Host ${ROBOT_ALIAS}_claude
    HostName $ROBOT_IP
    User $ROBOT_USER
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/$KEY_NAME
    IdentitiesOnly yes

Host ${ROBOT_ALIAS}_me
    HostName $ROBOT_IP
    User $ROBOT_USER
    PubkeyAuthentication no
    PreferredAuthentications password
EOF

The robots' IP addresses are on IP Reservations. For the username, see Contacts.

docs.title: Make Sure Password Login Works (Robot)
docs.text:
Open a shell on the robot (SSH, or keyboard and monitor). Keep this terminal open for the whole guide.

sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication

If it prints passwordauthentication yes, skip to the next section. If it prints no, enable it with a drop-in file. The 01- prefix makes it win over other config files.

DROPIN=/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-human-password.conf

echo 'PasswordAuthentication yes' | sudo tee $DROPIN
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh
sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication

Warning

sshd -t must print nothing. If it prints an error, do not restart. Delete the file you just made. The last command must say yes. If it still says no, another config overrides it. Run grep -ri passwordauth /etc/ssh/.

Restarting ssh does not kill existing sessions.

docs.title: Test Password Login, Then Print the Public Key (Ground Station)
docs.text:
Open a new terminal on the ground station. Set the same alias you used above:

ROBOT_ALIAS=homebrew02

ssh ${ROBOT_ALIAS}_me

Danger

You must get a password prompt and a normal shell. If you do not, stop here and fix it. Do not continue.

Type exit, then print the public key line and copy it:

KEY_NAME=claude_robot_key

cat ~/.ssh/$KEY_NAME.pub

docs.title: Prepare the Robot and Create the Wrapper (Robot)
docs.text:
Use your still-open robot shell. Set the names (the same KEY_COMMENT as above):

KEY_COMMENT=claude-robot-debug
WRAPPER=$HOME/bin/ssh-wrapper.sh
LOG_FILE=$HOME/logs/ssh-claude.log

Check that sudo needs a password. This must print nothing:

sudo -l | grep -i nopasswd

Warning

If it prints a line, remove that NOPASSWD entry (sudo visudo, or the file in /etc/sudoers.d/). A password-protected sudo is your hard stop for the agent.

Back up authorized_keys:

mkdir -p ~/.ssh ~/bin ~/logs
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
touch ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
cp ~/.ssh/authorized_keys ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.bak

Create the wrapper. It refuses interactive shells and logs every command and its exit code:

printf 'LOG=%q\n' "$LOG_FILE" > $WRAPPER
cat >> $WRAPPER <<'EOF'
if [ -z "$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND" ]; then
  echo "interactive shells disabled for this key" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "=== $(date -Is) CMD: $SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND" >> "$LOG"
bash -c "$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND" 2>&1 | tee -a "$LOG"
rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
echo "EXIT: $rc" >> "$LOG"
exit "$rc"
EOF
sed -i '1i #!/bin/bash' $WRAPPER
chmod +x $WRAPPER

docs.title: Install the Restricted Key (Robot)
docs.text:
First, set the public key. Paste the whole line you copied between the quotes:

PUBKEY='ssh-ed25519 AAAA...paste-here... claude-robot-debug'

Make sure the file ends in a newline, so the new entry does not merge into the last line:

[ -n "$(tail -c1 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys)" ] && echo >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Append the restricted entry:

printf 'command="%s",no-pty,no-port-forwarding,no-X11-forwarding,no-agent-forwarding %s\n' "$WRAPPER" "$PUBKEY" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Verify. The last line must start with command="/home/:

tail -n 1 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Count how many lines contain this key. It must print 1:

KEY_BLOB=$(echo "$PUBKEY" | awk '{print $2}')
grep -cF "$KEY_BLOB" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Warning

If the count is 2 or more, the same key also exists without restrictions, and the unrestricted entry wins. Show the line numbers:

grep -nF "$KEY_BLOB" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Delete the line that does not start with command= (replace N with its line number), then run the count again:

LINE=N
sed -i "${LINE}d" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

docs.title: Unlock the Key and Test (Ground Station)
docs.text:
Set the names:

KEY_NAME=claude_robot_key
ROBOT_ALIAS=homebrew02

Check for a running SSH agent. If this prints nothing, start one:

echo $SSH_AUTH_SOCK

eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

Unlock the key. Enter the passphrase. It locks again by itself after 8 hours.

ssh-add -t 8h ~/.ssh/$KEY_NAME

Run the tests:

ssh ${ROBOT_ALIAS}_claude "echo hello; whoami"
ssh ${ROBOT_ALIAS}_claude "docker ps"
ssh ${ROBOT_ALIAS}_claude
ssh ${ROBOT_ALIAS}_me

Expected results, in order:

  1. hello and your username.
  2. Docker output (if Docker is installed).
  3. A refusal such as PTY allocation request failed. This is correct.
  4. A password prompt and a full interactive shell.

On the robot, confirm the log recorded the commands:

tail $LOG_FILE

Plain ssh <robot> without an alias offers the agent's restricted key and hits the same refusal. Always use the _me alias for yourself.

Repeat the alias, password, key and test sections for each robot.

docs.title: Use It with Claude Code
docs.text:
Start Claude Code from a ground station shell where the SSH agent is loaded. Tell it to run non-interactive commands only, in the form ssh <robot>_claude "<command>". Good first requests are to pull the logs of a container, find the cause of an error, or add logging to a node, rebuild it, and run it again.

Lock the SSH agent when you are done:

ssh-add -D

docs.title: Undo Everything
docs.text:
On the robot (through _me or the console), set the names:

KEY_COMMENT=claude-robot-debug
WRAPPER=$HOME/bin/ssh-wrapper.sh
LOG_FILE=$HOME/logs/ssh-claude.log

sed -i "/$KEY_COMMENT/d" ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
rm -f $WRAPPER $LOG_FILE

Only if you created the password drop-in earlier:

DROPIN=/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-human-password.conf
sudo rm -f $DROPIN
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh

Danger

Removing the password drop-in turns password login off again if it was off originally. Only do this if you have another way in (a different key, or physical access), and keep your shell open.

On the ground station, set the name:

KEY_NAME=claude_robot_key

ssh-add -d ~/.ssh/$KEY_NAME
rm -f ~/.ssh/$KEY_NAME ~/.ssh/$KEY_NAME.pub
nano ~/.ssh/config

In nano, delete the _claude and _me blocks for each robot.

docs.title: Recovery: If You Are Locked Out
docs.text:
Password login and the console do not depend on authorized_keys. In order of effort:

  1. Console: plug in HDMI and a USB keyboard, log in with your account password, and run the robot undo commands above.

  2. Other password path: if PasswordAuthentication is on, connect with:

    ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no user@robot-ip

  3. Offline edit: power off, mount the robot's SD card or NVMe on another Linux computer, and edit /home/<user>/.ssh/authorized_keys. Remove the agent's key line or restore authorized_keys.bak.

Common causes of key failures: ~/.ssh not 700, authorized_keys not 600, a broken or multi-line entry, or command= pointing to a script that does not exist or is not executable.

docs.title: Autonomy Park SITL
docs.text:
Draft. Still in development. The first release is expected in December 2026. Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-06Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

The Autonomy Park SITL is a simulation environment for testing robot-ready code. It is in development; a release for one quadcopter is expected in December 2026.

A SITL (software in the loop) is a simulation environment for testing robot-ready code before it runs on a real robot. The setup instructions, the commands, and the supported versions are in the repository's README.

The Repository Is Private

The Autonomy Park SITL repository is private. To see it, get access on GitHub Access.

Autonomy Park SITL

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
It is still in development.

  • Quadcopters: it supports one Homebrew or one generic quadcopter. Multi-agent simulation is not supported. A release for this is expected in December 2026.
  • Unitree quadrupeds, and ground robots such as the Husky A200 and the Jackal UGV: simulation is in development, and is expected in March 2027.

Anyone using the Astros or Homebrews for offboard control must simulate in the SITL first: see Lab Rules.

docs.title: GitHub Contribution Guide
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

How to commit, branch, review, tag, and archive code in our GitHub organization, and when a repository is public or private. Read it before you push.

Our code lives in the UFL-Autonomy-Park GitHub organization. To get access to the private repositories, see GitHub Access.

docs.title: Commits
docs.text:
Use Conventional Commits. Start each commit message with a type, then a short description:

feat: add a landing-pad detector
fix: stop the node from crashing when the lidar drops out
docs: explain how to calibrate the camera

Common types are feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, and chore. Keep each commit to one change.

docs.title: Branches and Pull Requests
docs.text:
• Develop every feature on its own branch. Do not commit features straight to main.
  • Open a pull request when the feature is tested and ready for development, meaning it is ready for the rest of us to build on.
  • Test before you open the pull request, and say in it how you tested.

docs.title: Version Tags
docs.text: Tag each release with a version number, such as v1.2.0, so anyone can return to the exact code behind an experiment.

docs.title: Archiving Old Code
docs.text: When a repository is no longer maintained, archive it on GitHub instead of deleting it. Archived code stays readable, and the history of past papers and projects is kept.

docs.title: The README
docs.text: Every README must say which paper or project the repository is for.

docs.title: Public and Private
docs.text:
• Keep shared code public.
  • Keep anything that will go in a paper private until it is published.
  • Never change a repository between public and private without asking first. Ask a person on the Contacts page.

docs.title: IP Reservations
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-06Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

Every device on the Autonomy Park and Indoor Lab networks has a reserved IP address. The addresses are not published on the wiki; the sheets below have them.

The IP addresses are not published on the wiki. Using a robot needs a username and password as well, and we do not publish those.

Two Separate Networks

The Autonomy Park and the Indoor Lab each have their own network, and both use the 192.168.1.x range. The same address can mean a different device in each.

Autonomy Park IP Reservations Sheet Indoor Lab IP Reservations Sheet

To fix a device's IP address at the Autonomy Park, see Reserving a Static IP Address. To get access to the lists, see Contacts.

docs.title: Quadcopter Flight Practice
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

Practice flying with the Liftoff simulator on Steam before you fly a real quadcopter. You need an RC controller and a computer.

A quadcopter in Liftoff (screenshot from the game).

Liftoff on Steam

Liftoff: FPV Drone Racing is a good simulation of flying a quadcopter by hand. It is the best place to practice before you fly one of our robots, because a crash costs nothing.

docs.title: What You Need
docs.text:
• An RC controller, such as our Taranis X9D (with a USB-B cable). Liftoff only works with a game or radio controller, not a keyboard.
  • A computer: Mac, Windows, or Linux.
  • A Steam account. The Steam login for the lab is in the Autonomy Park Bitwarden. If you need access, see Contacts.

docs.title: How to Connect the Controller
docs.text: The Taranis X9D connects to the computer over USB. You need a USB-B cable.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: When you are ready to fly a real quadcopter, read Flying Manually for the Homebrews or Flying Manually for the Astros.

docs.title: Lab Notes
docs.text: Only what the vendor guides lack. The steps for the simulation setup come in this order: ROS 2, QGroundControl, Gazebo, PX4, then MAVROS.

docs.title: Ubuntu
docs.text:
All the park's equipment requires Ubuntu 22.04.5 (Jammy Jellyfish) for complete functionality of the park's resources (ROS 2 Humble needs it). Keep the version you installed and never update Ubuntu.

For a complete tutorial on running Linux in a virtual machine on Windows for a general ROS 2 project, see Ubuntu in VMware (written steps) or Ubuntu in VirtualBox (video). Apple Silicon Macs are not covered by either: they need an ARM-based Ubuntu, and some things, such as GPU acceleration for Gazebo, will not work.

Virtual Machine Disk Space

For general tutorials and work, 20 GB of allocated disk space works well. For larger projects with PX4 and Gazebo, 20 GB is not sufficient. Allocate a minimum of 40 GB, and 50 to 60 GB for good overall performance.

docs.title: ROS 2 Humble
docs.text:
The installation steps are exactly the same as in the vendor guide linked above. A video walkthrough:

To test the installation, run the talker example from the vendor guide in one terminal:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker

Run the listener in another terminal:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener

The talker should say it is publishing messages and the listener should say it heard them. This verifies both the C++ and Python APIs.

docs.title: QGroundControl (QGC)
docs.text:
QGC 5.1.x and Later Has No Ubuntu 22.04 Binary

QGC 5.1.x and later do not provide binaries for Ubuntu 22.04. On Ubuntu 22.04 you must build QGC from scratch. QGC 5.0.8 is fine to use for the foreseeable future.

In a new terminal, add yourself to the dialout group, remove ModemManager, and install the packages QGC needs:

sudo usermod -a -G dialout $USER
sudo apt-get remove modemmanager -y
sudo apt install gstreamer1.0-plugins-bad gstreamer1.0-libav gstreamer1.0-gl -y
sudo apt install libfuse2 -y
sudo apt install libxcb-xinerama0 libxkbcommon-x11-0 libxcb-cursor-dev -y

Download QGroundControl.AppImage from the download link, move it to a folder of your choice (for example ~/Downloads), make it executable, and run it:

chmod +x ~/Downloads/QGroundControl.AppImage
~/Downloads/QGroundControl.AppImage

docs.title: Gazebo
docs.text: PX4 SITL uses Gazebo Harmonic. Install it following the vendor guide linked above.

docs.title: Planned Change: MAVROS to uXRCE-DDS
docs.text:
The lab plans to move offboard control of the quadcopters from MAVROS to the Micro XRCE-DDS Agent (uXRCE-DDS), PX4's native connection to ROS 2. Nothing changes yet: MAVROS is still the path described on this page as of 2026-10-21.

Why: MAVROS does not support torque-level offboard commands, and uXRCE-DDS does. In the lab's current setup, though, using uXRCE-DDS means giving up RTK. As of PX4 1.17.0 (and so 1.16.2), the Micro XRCE-DDS Agent exposes no topic for serving RTK corrections. With MAVROS, an NTRIP client on a companion computer publishes them to <mavros_namespace>/mavros/gps_rtk/send_rtcm.

A PX4 change Max test flew for the PX4 devs addresses that. PX4 pull request #29368 will let ROS 2 applications send RTK (RTCM) corrections to PX4 over uXRCE-DDS. As of 2026-11-10 it is merged, butis not part of any stable PX4 release (the release that will include it: Unknown). To experiment with torque-level control together with RTK, you must build mainline PX4 and port every parameter to the current PX4 parameter reference.

docs.title: MAVROS
docs.text:
In a new terminal, install MAVROS and its dependencies:

sudo apt install ros-humble-mavros ros-humble-mavros-extras
sudo apt install ros-humble-geographic-msgs
sudo apt install geographiclib-tools
sudo apt install libgeographic-dev
sudo apt install geographiclib-doc

Create the GeographicLib directories if they do not exist:

sudo mkdir -p /usr/share/GeographicLib/geoids
sudo mkdir -p /usr/share/GeographicLib/gravity
sudo mkdir -p /usr/share/GeographicLib/magnetic

Install the egm96-5 dataset manually:

sudo geographiclib-get-geoids egm96-5

With PX4 running in a separate terminal (see above), launch MAVROS. It connects to PX4 over MAVLink. Autonomy Park SITL does this for you.

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ros2 launch mavros px4.launch fcu_url:="udp://:14540@127.0.0.1:14557"

docs.title: Ubuntu in VirtualBox
docs.text:
Draft. Only a video so far. The written steps are not written yet. Written by Wyatt CrossUpdated 2026-11-06Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

A video walkthrough for installing Ubuntu 22.04 in a VirtualBox virtual machine. There are no written steps yet.

Apple Silicon Macs Are Not Covered

There is no guide for Apple Silicon Macs, because they need an ARM-based Ubuntu. ROS 2 supports it, but some things, such as GPU acceleration for Gazebo, will not work. We have not tested these virtual machines with ROS on a Mac.

Use Ubuntu 22.04.5, and never update it (see Ubuntu in VMware for why).

The written steps: Unknown

The same installation in VMware, with written steps, is on Ubuntu in VMware.

docs.title: Ubuntu in VMware
docs.text:
Draft. Moved from a PDF dated 2025-01-24. The steps are transcribed from it and have not been re-run by Max. Written by Keith Currier, Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-06Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

Runs on: Windows. How to install Ubuntu 22.04.5 in a VMware virtual machine on a Windows computer, so you can do the ROS 2 tutorials without deleting Windows. There is also a video walkthrough for VirtualBox: see Ubuntu in VirtualBox.

Apple Silicon Macs Are Not Covered

There is no guide for Apple Silicon Macs, because they need an ARM-based Ubuntu. ROS 2 supports it, but some things, such as GPU acceleration for Gazebo, will not work. We have not tested these virtual machines with ROS on a Mac.

A virtual machine (VMware) lets you run Linux on your Windows computer without deleting the operating system. This guide gets Ubuntu running so you can do the ROS 2 tutorials. The same installation in VirtualBox, with a video, is on Ubuntu in VirtualBox. The other software the lab uses is on Software We Use.

Never Update Ubuntu

Use Ubuntu 22.04.5, and do not update it. ROS 2 Humble needs it. When Ubuntu offers to upgrade, always decline.

docs.title: Install VMware
docs.text:
1. Download VMware Workstation Pro from the VMware link on Software We Use. This guide used version 17. If it asks, use it for personal use.

  2. Run the installer. The setup wizard is straightforward and needs no special changes.

    One suggestion: turn off VMware checking for updates on startup, and update only when you open the Workstation.

  3. Open VMware Workstation. The first time, it looks like this:

docs.title: Download Ubuntu
docs.text:
1. Download Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish), the 64-bit PC (AMD64) desktop image. The file is called ubuntu-22.04.5-desktop-amd64.iso and lands in your downloads.

  2. Move the file to a folder you will remember, so you know its path.

docs.title: Create the Virtual Machine
docs.text:
1. In VMware, choose Create a New Virtual Machine. Select Installer disc image file (iso) and give the path to the Ubuntu file. VMware should say that Ubuntu 64-bit 22.04.5 was detected.

  2. Fill in your name, a username and a password for the virtual machine.

  3. When it asks how large the disk should be, leave the standard size (20 GB) for just the ROS tutorials. If you need to flash NVIDIA Jetsons or do more with your VM, select 100 GB. Larger projects need more: see the note on disk space in Software We Use.

  4. Finish the wizard. The virtual machine boots, and the Ubuntu installer starts.

docs.title: Install Ubuntu
docs.text:
1. Use the standard settings. They are enough to learn ROS 2.

  2. Ubuntu asks whether to erase the entire disk. This is fine here: the disk space belongs to the virtual machine, which you allocated already. Make sure you followed all the steps above and that Ubuntu is open in VMware Workstation, then start the installation.

  3. Enter your name, a computer name, a username and a password.

    Keep the computer name short and easy to remember, because you will see it in the terminal when you work in Linux and ROS 2. For example, if your name is Bob Murray, the computer name could be bmurr. Make the username and password easy to remember, since you use them to log in when the virtual machine starts or after it has been idle.

  4. Let the installation continue. It restarts the virtual machine, then asks you to log in with the username and password you set. Continue the setup until you see the "You're ready to go" screen.

  5. Ubuntu will prompt you to update. Do not update. Click Don't Upgrade. Keep Ubuntu 22.04.5 to work on ROS 2 Humble.

  6. Ubuntu is now fully installed. Add the terminal to your favorites so it stays on the taskbar: click Show Applications at the bottom of the taskbar, then right-click the terminal and favorite it.

docs.title: Next: ROS 2
docs.text:
Open the terminal and install ROS 2 by following the official Humble guide. A video walkthrough is on Software We Use. Then do the tutorials.

ROS 2 Humble Installation ROS 2 Humble Tutorials

docs.title: Upgrading ROS 2
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

Why a ROS 2 upgrade is a months-long project, and how to find everything that must be checked first. Read it before you plan one.

Do Not Take a ROS 2 Upgrade Lightly

Updating ROS 2 requires upgrading every computer, every Docker container, and most of the robots. This will take months or over a year to do, test, and debug.

ROS 2 is released in lockstep with Ubuntu LTS versions: each ROS 2 long-term release is built for one Ubuntu LTS release, so a new ROS 2 distribution means a new Ubuntu on the computers too. The list of distributions and their end-of-life dates is on the ROS 2 releases page.

docs.title: Where We Are
docs.text:
ROS 2 Humble is scheduled to reach end of life in 2027. We will likely switch to the latest stable ROS 2 distribution after this. Since this requires massive effort, we will delay it as long as possible, though.

Approval Needed

Dr. Kamalapurkar owns all robots and thus approves major upgrades like these.

docs.title: Finding What an Upgrade Touches
docs.text: Software We Use was made to help you check all of the many places whose compatibility with a ROS 2 upgrade must be checked, or reworked from scratch, before an upgrade.

docs.title: What Is Safe to Upgrade
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-06Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

Which software and firmware you can upgrade without breaking our code, and which need serious expertise. When in doubt, do not upgrade.

Safe here means reasonably safe: nothing will break if you use the same code, and no documentation will need to change. Anything marked as needing testing must be tested on a single robot first.

Component Safe to Upgrade? Notes Emlid receiver firmware ✅ Safe Emlid Flow app ✅ Safe QGroundControl ✅ Safe Here4 firmware ✅ Safe Auterion CLI ✅ Safe Minor apt upgrades ✅ Safe A minor apt upgrade may also update MAVROS, which is not safe. MAVROS ❌ Not safe Needs testing. Docker ⚠️ Sometimes Some upgrades (such as apt upgrades) are safe, others are not. Needs testing. PX4 ❌ Not safe Port the parameters by hand: see Upgrading PX4 Firmware. JetPack ❌ Not safe Needs a revised homebrew_docker. ROS 2 distribution ❌ Never Ubuntu version ❌ Never See Software We Use. OptiTrack Motive ❌ Cannot be upgraded Our license, and so our access to updates, expired. If the license key is lost, or Motive stops working (for example after a forced Windows upgrade), replacing it is not safe: it would force a switch from VRPN to NatNet. Freefly Astro software ⚠️ Sometimes It depends on if Freefly updates the minor version of the underlying APX4. All updates tested thus far have not changed the PX4 version and have been fine.

docs.title: Planned Changes
docs.text:
These are optional and not urgent. Whoever wants to spend the time, and the need for it, decides when.

  • MAVROS to uXRCE-DDS for the Homebrews, after PX4 1.19.0 is released. PX4 1.19.0 is a long way off. See the Case Study: Porting the Homebrew Parameters to PX4 Main.
    • homebrew_docker contains aero_common, which makes offboard programs more modular. aero_common will need updates for the switch. Once they are tested in the Autonomy Park SITL, it should pretty much work.
    • One caveat: the MicroStrain ntrip_client in homebrew_docker uses MAVROS. Using XRCE (a brand-new feature) needs code Max wrote in the rtk_tests_for_px4_1_18 branch of homebrew_docker, which would have to be merged into main.

docs.title: Contacts
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-21

At a glance

Who to ask about the Autonomy Park and the Indoor Lab: the PI and the lab managers.

These three people are the contacts for the Autonomy Park, the Indoor Lab, and this wiki. If a page tells you to ask someone, ask one of them.

docs.title: Edit the Wiki
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-21

At a glance

All users of the Autonomy Park and the Indoor Lab are expected to track their hardware issues, document useful facts, and correct errors in this wiki. This guide teaches how to edit it.

This wiki is a folder of Markdown files in a GitHub repository. MkDocs with the Material theme turns them into the website. Pushing to the main branch publishes the site automatically.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
You need three tools.

Tool What it is for Git Versioning and sharing your changes Git LFS Stores large files (PDFs, photos, videos) outside the normal Git history uv Installs the correct Python and every package the wiki needs, at exact locked versions

You do not install Python or MkDocs yourself. uv does that for you. Everything on this page runs on your own computer.

Linux / WSLmacOSWindows

Install Git and Git LFS:

sudo apt install git git-lfs

Install uv:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Install all three tools:

brew install git git-lfs uv

Install Git. This also installs Git LFS:

winget install --id Git.Git -e

Install uv:

winget install --id astral-sh.uv -e

Turn on Git LFS. Do this once per computer:

git lfs install

Check that all three tools respond with a version number:

git --version
git lfs version
uv --version

Turn on Git LFS before you clone

Without Git LFS, PDFs and photos download as tiny text files, and any large file you add goes into the normal Git history, where it stays permanently and slows down everyone's clones. See Large Files (Git LFS).

docs.title: Get the Wiki
docs.text:
You need access to the UFL-Autonomy-Park GitHub organization. Ask one of the people on the Contacts page to add you.

Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/UFL-Autonomy-Park/apark_wiki.git

From here on, run every command inside the apark_wiki folder. Enter it and install the exact package versions the wiki uses. This creates a private environment in .venv/:

cd apark_wiki
uv sync

Preview the site on your computer:

uv run mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/. The page reloads every time you save a file. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

Read the terminal output

The preview prints WARNING lines in the terminal for broken links and missing files. Fix them before you push. A clean build prints none. The boxed notice from the Material team about MkDocs 2.0 is expected and is not about our site.

docs.title: Change or Add a Page
docs.text:
Pages are .md files under docs/. Each folder is a section in the sidebar. To add a page, put a new .md file in an existing folder, or create a folder for a new section.

Start every page with a title block:

---
title: Your Title Here
---

For Markdown syntax, see the Markdown Guide. For boxes such as notes and warnings, see the Material admonitions reference.

docs.title: Links, Images, and PDFs
docs.text:
Use paths relative to the page you are editing.

A PDF sits in the same folder as the page that uses it and is linked by file name:

[Battery Manual](tattu-manual.pdf)

An image goes in docs/images/, in a folder named for its topic. From a page in docs/start-here/, the path looks like this:

![Autonomy Park robots](../images/index/robot-banner.jpg)

Count the ../ by how deep the page is. A page in docs/robots/quadcopters/homebrew/ needs ../../../images/ at the start of the path. If an image does not show up in the preview, the number of ../ is almost always the reason. Always write alt text (the text in the square brackets) that says what the picture shows.

Another page is linked by its .md file:

[Configure the Bebop network](../robots/quadcopters/parrot-bebop-2/connecting-to-wifi.md)

docs.title: Large Files (Git LFS)
docs.text:
Git LFS keeps the repository small. These file types are stored with LFS automatically, as listed in .gitattributes:

.pdf .jpg .mp4 .mov .heic .avif

Use one format per kind of file: photos as .jpg (1600 px or less on the long side), screenshots as .png, diagrams as .svg, videos as short muted .mp4 clips (longer videos go on YouTube), and vendor manuals as .pdf. Never use .webp.

If you turned on Git LFS (see Requirements), you do nothing special. Add the file and commit as usual.

  • Save photos as .jpg (not .jpeg) and resize them to about 1600 pixels on the long side before adding them.
  • Export a real .jpg from your photo tool. Renaming a .jpeg file does not convert it.
  • Anything that is not one of the types above, such as .png screenshots, stays in regular Git. Keep those small.

To confirm a new file went into LFS, list the LFS files. Your file should appear:

git lfs ls-files

A PDF or image shows as a few lines of text

The file is an LFS pointer, which means the real file was never downloaded. Download it:

git lfs install
git lfs pull

docs.title: Publish Your Changes
docs.text:
Stage all changes

git add

Commmit changes

git commit -m "docs: <what you changed and why>"

Push changes

git push -u origin <branch-name>
- Write what and why in the commit message. Start it with docs: for content, fix: for corrections, or feat: for new sections in the style of Conventional Commits. - Update the page when you change a robot. If you changed a robot's configuration, network, or software, document it here. Anyone who inherits the robot depends on it.

docs.title: Lab Rules
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-10Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

The rules everyone follows in the lab, in one short list. Read it before you fly, charge a battery, or use anything.

docs.title: General Rules
docs.text:
• All hardware belongs to Dr. Kamalapurkar. We do not lend hardware to anyone outside the SCC roster.
  • No removing robots/equipment from the Autonomy Park. SCC Lab Members are exempt.
  • Do not leave the Emlid RTK units outside. It's not waterproof and it's expensive to replace. Bring inside when done.
  • Read the documentation for a robot before you use it. Every robot has pages in the Robots tab. Read all of them first.
  • Safety glasses are required outdoors.
  • No operating robots in weather. Rain and high wind ruin equipment. Bring it inside.
  • Minimize spectators. Our labs are for research and must be shared. Lots of unnecessary workers can become a safety issue.
  • Every robot must have an RC with a kill switch. For quadcopters, a disarm switch will not cut it. For ground robots, this usually means a dead-man switch.
  • Keep things nice. Put all robots away when done, close the blinds, and turn off all lights.
  • Report all crashes and injuries to Dr. Kamalapurkar. See Report an Incident.

docs.title: Flying
docs.text:
• No flying vehicles outside the net. It's illegal. No exceptions.
  • Never enter the net while a quadcopter is armed or flying. Disarm it first.
  • No benchwork on drones with batteries and propellers on at the same time. We've had people get seriously injured by unexpected spinning.
  • Watch flying vehicles at all times. Don't get distracted with your code or a visualizer.

docs.title: LiPo Batteries
docs.text:
• Never leave a charging battery unattended. Charge only with the approved charger, on a non-flammable surface.
  • Never charge or fly a battery that is hot, damaged, or swollen.
  • Never charge above 4.2 V per cell, and never discharge below 3.0 V per cell. Any cell outside those limits is permanently damaged. Chargers generally prevent over-charging. Only you can prevent over-discharging.
  • Never puncture a battery, carry it by its leads, or throw it in the trash.
  • Put a dropped, damaged, swollen, old, or wrongly charged battery in the ammo can, and tell a lab manager right away. Tape any severed leads first. The Autonomy Park's ammo can is in the storage shed by the Venom chargers. The Indoor Lab's is on a bottom shelf in the Indoor Lab.
  • Don't fight LiPo battery fires. Get to safety and call 911. Never use an extinguisher, water, or sand.

docs.title: Hardware-Specific
docs.text:
• Those using Dr. Kamalapurkar's drones (Astros and Homebrews) for off-board control must simulate in Autonomy Park SITL first for safety reasons.
  • No custom firmware/autopilots. Especially for quadcopters, this is a safety risk.
  • Control barrier functions (CBFs) are required for multi-agent experiments. CBFs for offboard control do not exist yet, and more RFD 900x radios must be bought, so multi-agent experiments are not possible right now.
  • Every Homebrew needs an RFD 900x radio to fly for safety reasons. Otherwise, your off-board program is the sole failure point for getting a drone to land safely (very dangerous!).

docs.title: Soldering
docs.text:
• No leaded solder. Leaded waste requires a pick-up. You also cannot mix lead and lead-free solder.
  • Wash your hands after soldering. Treat it as though it were leaded.
  • Replace the iron in the holder and turn it off when done. It's a fire risk.

Safety Report an Incident Contacts

docs.title: Lab Spaces and Dimensions
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-03

At a glance

Know how much room you have before planning an experiment. This page gives the usable size of the Indoor Lab and the Autonomy Park, and the axes of the Indoor Lab's motion-capture system.

The SCC Lab runs two spaces. The Autonomy Park is the outdoor space, a university resource. The Indoor Lab in MAE-A 313 is the indoor motion-capture lab.

docs.title: Autonomy Park
docs.text:
The Autonomy Park from the air.

The Autonomy Park is 240 ft (73 m) long, 60 ft (18 m) wide, and 20 ft (7 m) tall.

The Autonomy Park is located at the UF Energy Park, which Apple and Google Maps call the UF Solar Park. It's a fenced, gated facility.

Google Maps Apple Maps

The Autonomy Park from above. The netted area is in the middle.

docs.title: Autonomy Park Frame
docs.text:
The Autonomy Park frame is the frame used in the aero_common and other repositories.

  • Origin: the center of the Autonomy Park, at 29.628147° N, 82.360333° W. This coordinate was chosen by Max Gardenswartz on Google Earth very carefully and works well in experiments. Use it everywhere unless you really know what you're doing and find it needs to be (minorly) adjusted (e.g., testing CBFs with quadcopters).
  • x axis: along the long side of the Park (240 ft, 73 m). It is rotated 33.83072° southward from a true ENU frame (east, north, up).
  • y axis: along the short side of the Park (60 ft, 18 m), pointing northeast-ish.
  • z axis: up.
  • Sheds: both sheds sit at the -x end of the Park. The main shed is the one closer to the net; the storage shed is farther out.

To get access to either space, see Lab Access.

docs.title: Indoor Lab
docs.text:
Safety Nets Are Planned

Safety nets are planned as a future safety feature of the Indoor Lab. As of 2026-10-21 they are not installed. When and where they will go: Unknown.

The Indoor Lab (MAE-A 313). The black units on the ceiling are the motion-capture cameras.

The Indoor Lab (MAE-A 313) has about 18 ft by 9 ft by 44 ft (5.5 m, 2.75 m, 13.5 m) of space for autonomous experiments.

The origin of the mocap system was calibrated so that, the space is divided around it as follows:

Axis Positive direction Space on the positive side Space on the negative side Total x From inside the building out the west window 9 ft (2.75 m) 9 ft (2.75 m) 18 ft (5.5 m) y Up 7 ft (2.1 m) None. The origin is on the floor. 7 ft (2.1 m) z North 20 ft (6 m) 24 ft (7.5 m) 44 ft (13.5 m)

Plan view, drawn to scale from the table above. West is on the left because north is at the top.

These axes are not ENU

The axes do not follow a convention like ENU. They are simply how OptiTrack Motive, the mocap software, sets them up. See Mocap Calibration for how the origin and axes are set.

docs.title: Report an Incident
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-06Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

What to do after a crash, an injury, or a LiPo fire: who to call and who to tell, in order.

docs.title: Equipment Crash
docs.text: If only equipment is involved (for example, a quadcopter crashes inside the net and the landing gear breaks, but no one is hurt), report it to Dr. Kamalapurkar.

docs.title: Injury
docs.text:
Do these in order:

  1. Get medical attention immediately. For a serious or life-threatening injury, go to the emergency room or call 911, especially if you are alone. For a minor injury, go to urgent care.
  2. Tell Dr. Kamalapurkar.
  3. Submit an incident report with UF Environmental Health and Safety (EHS).
  4. Call AmeriSys at 1-800-455-2079 if you are employed by the University (for example, a graduate student researcher with a stipend). This is so you can get paid later if your injury causes disability or lifelong problems.

Submit an EHS Incident Report

docs.title: LiPo Fire
docs.text: Get away and call 911. Do not try to fight it. Never use an extinguisher, water, or sand. See Lab Rules.

docs.title: After a Crash
docs.text: Never enter the net while a quadcopter is armed. See Lab Rules.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Written by Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-11-09Autonomy ParkIndoor Lab

At a glance

Read the Lab Rules and finish the safety training before you work in the Autonomy Park. Access is denied until you finish the safety video and pass the quiz!

Read the Lab Rules Before Working in the Autonomy Park

Read the Lab Rules before you work in the Autonomy Park or fly any robot. Complete the training below first.

Lab Rules

docs.title: Mandatory Training
docs.text: All access requests will be DENIED if you do not complete the online training first.

docs.title: Quiz
docs.text:
After the video, you must take the following quiz and score at least 80% for your training to be considered complete! Reach out to Dr. Kamalapurkar and a lab manager will add you to the Canvas.

Canvas Link to the Quiz

docs.title: EHS Trainings: Indoor Lab Only
docs.text:
If you need the Indoor Lab, you must also complete two UF Environmental Health and Safety (EHS) trainings. The Autonomy Park does not need them.

Training Why It Is Required How Often EHS 809: Hazardous Waste Management Required for all UF labs Repeat every 365 days EHS 869: Chemical Hygiene Plan The Indoor Lab has chemicals (isopropyl alcohol and hot glue) Once, ever

To take either training:

  1. Go to UF MyTraining.
  2. Click Continue with GatorLink and sign in if prompted.
  3. In the search bar (top right corner), search for the course number (EHS809 or EHS869).
  4. There should be one result: Hazardous Waste Management (EHS 809) or Chemical Hygiene Plan (EHS 869). Click on it.
  5. Click Start. Once you start, you can always resume later.
  6. Allow pop-ups, or the training will not open.

UF MyTraining

Then request access: Lab Access.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Written by Brandon Fallin, Max GardenswartzUpdated 2026-10-21Autonomy Park

At a glance

The lab's shared Chrome profile and the Bitwarden password manager. Use them so that accounts and bookmarks stay consistent across lab computers.

docs.title: Chrome
docs.text: All of the Autonomy Park bookmarks and accounts are saved in our Google Chrome profile. Log in using the Autonomy Park email and password (the lab managers on Contacts can give them to you). Use Chrome on all Autonomy Park computers to keep things consistent. Most things you want for the Autonomy Park are bookmarked!

docs.title: Bitwarden
docs.text:
Do not use the default Autonomy Park password for any user account. Generate a strong password and save it to Bitwarden. This is installed as an extension in our Chrome profile. To save a new login, do the following:

Navigate to the site which you need a new login for. In this example, we'll use reddit.com. Open the Bitwarden extension. Click the +New button and then the Login button.

Fill in the username field and click the generator button in the password field to create a strong unique password.

Copy the password to your clipboard. Click Use this password. Then, click Save.
